In the earlier chapters we computed stresses and displacements for a given structure. Here we ask the opposite question: what should the structure be, so that it is the best one? The wall truss of chapters 4 and 7 was computed with bars of cross-section 100 mm\(^2\). Its largest stress is 166,7 MPa, and the yield limit of the steel is 220 MPa (chapter 3). The bars are therefore stronger than they need to be. By how much may we thin them, so that as little steel as possible is used, and how do we find it by computing instead of by trying?

The chapter is named after two words. Optimization (optimizacija) comes from the Latin optimus, the best: to optimize means to find the best among the possibilities. Structure (konstrukcija) comes from the Latin construere, to build together: it is a load-carrying assembly of parts, built so that it carries its load. It matters because the weight and the price of a structure are proportional to the amount of material, and because the first idea we try is almost never the best.

The chapter promises three things. First we write the question "what is best" in a form that a computer understands, and say when a best solution exists at all. Then we prove how the best solution is recognized, and show the procedures that find it: for trusses, for a rod whose cross-section varies along its length, and for a plate in which we search for where the material should be at all. For every procedure we say what was neglected and when it fails.

29.1 The optimization problem (naloga optimizacije)

The usual procedure in practice is this: the designer proposes a shape, checks the requirements, for example that the stress does not exceed the allowed one, and if the shape does not meet them or is too heavy, proposes a new one. The procedure repeats and is led mostly by experience (CHK, PDF p. 12). Mathematical optimization differs in that it writes the requirements as constraints and "as good as possible" as a function that assigns a number to every idea (CHK, PDF p. 12-13). So the computer can compare ideas by itself. First let us see what has to be written down, on a truss we already know.

Let us draw the truss of section 4.1.4: bar \(AC\) is horizontal and 4 m long, bar \(BC\) is inclined and 5 m long, both are pinned to the wall and joined at the joint \(C\) by a pin. The bars are steel, with modulus of elasticity \(E = 196\) GPa (definition 3.1). A load hangs at the joint, \(F = 10\) kN. The cross-section of a bar is the area of its section perpendicular to the axis. We write the cross-sections of both bars as \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). These are numbers that the designer chooses, and they are what we vary in this problem, so we call them design variables (projektni spremenljivki). The name says that they are part of the design (projekt): with them the structure is determined once the geometry is chosen. The letter \(A\) has two meanings here. Without an index it is a point (a pin), with the index of a bar it is the area of a cross-section. An area always has an index.

To every choice of cross-sections the truss responds. The joint \(C\) is at rest, so the sum of the forces on it is zero (Newton's second law for a body in equilibrium). The forces of the bars on the pin are \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}\), with the axial force \(N\) of lemma 4.5. Since bar \(AC\) pushes horizontally on the pin, bar \(BC\) pulls it towards \(B\) and the load pulls it down, equilibrium in the directions \(x\) and \(y\) gives, as in section 4.1.4, \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN. The two equilibrium equations alone determine both forces, so the forces in the bars do not depend on the cross-sections. The cross-sections determine how the bars lengthen, and with that the displacement of the joint. The displacement of the joint \(C\) is magnified in the figure and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -10{,}714\) mm is its vertical component. The stress in a bar is the force per area of the cross-section, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{AC}} = N_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{BC}} = N_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), so for cross-sections of 100 mm\(^2\) it is \(-133{,}3\) MPa and \(166{,}7\) MPa.

The displacement and the forces of the bars, which the truss gives in response to a choice of cross-sections, we call the state. And what does "best" mean? We decide on two things. The measure is the volume of the steel \(V = L_{\mathrm{AC}}A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), because at a given density of steel the mass and the cost are proportional to the volume. The requirements are three: the stress in neither bar may exceed the allowed one \(\sigma_0\), the downward displacement of the joint may not exceed \(\delta\), and the cross-sections must be positive.

Let us write this in general. We take a structure with \(n\) design variables and a state described by the numbers in a column \(\vek d\). For a truss these are the displacements of the joints, as in chapter 7, and the forces in the bars are computed from them.

Definition 29.1 Structural optimization problem (naloga optimizacije konstrukcije)
Motivation

We want to write down what we change in a structure, what changes by itself as a result, what we measure and what must hold.

A structural optimization problem (naloga optimizacije konstrukcije) is the statement

\[\begin{aligned} &\text{minimize} && f(\vek\alpha, \vek d) && \text{over } \vek\alpha \in \mathbb R^n \text{ and } \vek d \in \mathbb R^m , \\ &\text{subject to} && g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek\alpha, \vek d) \le 0 , \quad i = 1, \dots, k , \\ & && \mat K(\vek\alpha)\,\vek d = \vek F , \end{aligned} \tag{29.1}\]

in which:

  1. \(\vek\alpha = (\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_{\mathrm{n}})\) is the column of design variables (projektne spremenljivke), \(n\) numbers that the designer chooses and that describe the structure: cross-sections of bars, thicknesses, coordinates of joints or the shape of an edge,
  2. \(\vek d\) is the column of state variables (spremenljivke stanja), \(m\) numbers that describe the response of the structure at a given \(\vek\alpha\): displacements of the joints, and from them forces and stresses,
  3. \(f\) is the objective function (ciljna funkcija), a function \(f \colon \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^m \to \mathbb R\) that assigns a number to every design, and smaller is better,
  4. \(g_1, \dots, g_{\mathrm{k}}\) are functions of the same kind, and the conditions \(g_{\mathrm{i}} \le 0\) are the constraints (omejitve). A constraint that depends on \(\vek d\) is a behavioural constraint (omejitev obnašanja), for example the largest stress or displacement. A constraint that depends only on \(\vek\alpha\) is a design constraint (projektna omejitev), for example the smallest cross-section,
  5. \(\mat K(\vek\alpha)\,\vek d = \vek F\) is the equilibrium constraint (ravnotežni pogoj). The matrix \(\mat K(\vek\alpha)\) of size \(m \times m\) is the part of the structure matrix (corollary 7.14) for the free unknowns, \(\vek F\) is the column of loads. In chapter 7 we called it \(\vek f\). Here we write it with a capital letter, because \(f\) is now the objective function.
Explanation

The conditions have only the form \(g_{\mathrm{i}} \le 0\), non-strict inequalities. An inequality \(g > 0\) can be written as \(-g \le 0\), an equation \(h = 0\) as the pair \(h \le 0\) and \(-h \le 0\). Strict inequalities (\(g < 0\)) do not occur in the problem. The positivity of the cross-sections is not such a constraint, because the inequality is strict. It says which designs have a meaning, since an area is positive, and we demand it separately (step 7 below). What it means that it is strict is shown by example 29.6. The letter \(g\) here means a constraint function and not the gravitational acceleration. The letter \(f\) is the objective function. In this chapter we do not use both at once.

Source: CHK §1.3 (PDF p. 13-14): objective function, design variable, state variable, behavioural and design constraints, equilibrium constraint \(\mat K(x)u = F(x)\). The notation with the columns \(\vek\alpha\) and \(\vek d\) is ours.

Let us write what the definition requires for our truss, step by step.

  1. There are \(n = 2\) design variables: \(\vek\alpha = (A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}})\).
  2. The pins \(A\) and \(B\) are fixed, so the joint \(C\) has two unknowns, \(\vek d = (u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}})\), \(m = 2\).
  3. The objective is the volume. The bar lengths are 4 m and \(\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2}\ \text{m} = 5\) m: \(f = 4\,A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5\,A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). If the cross-sections are in mm\(^2\), the volume is in cm\(^3\), because 1 mm\(^2 \cdot 1\) m = \(10^{-6}\) m\(^3\) = 1 cm\(^3\). With cross-sections of 100 mm\(^2\) each, \(f = 900\) cm\(^3\).
  4. By corollary 7.14 the equilibrium constraint is the sum of the bar matrices. The unit vectors of the bars are \((1, 0)\) for \(AC\) and \((0{,}8, -0{,}6)\) for \(BC\), so
    \[\mat K = \frac{EA_{\mathrm{AC}}}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \frac{EA_{\mathrm{BC}}}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 0{,}64 & -0{,}48 \\ -0{,}48 & 0{,}36 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \vek F = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -F \end{bmatrix} . \tag{29.2}\]
    For cross-sections of 100 mm\(^2\) each, \(\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix}\cdot 10^6\) N/m and the solution is \(\vek d = (-2{,}721, -10{,}714)\) mm, as in section 7.5.2.
  5. The behavioural constraint for stress: the axial force of a bar is \(N_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{EA_{\mathrm{e}}}{L_{\mathrm{e}}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot(\vek u_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek u_{\mathrm{i}})\) (section 7.5.2), so the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{e}} = N_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}} = E\,\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot(\vek u_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek u_{\mathrm{i}})/L_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{e}} = |\sigma_{\mathrm{e}}| - \sigma_0 \le 0\) for \(e = AC, BC\). We take \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa, the yield limit of steel (chapter 3), without a safety factor. This is an idealization: a factor, for example 1,5, would enlarge all cross-sections by that factor.
  6. The behavioural constraint for displacement: \(g_3 = -v_{\mathrm{C}} - \delta \le 0\), where \(\delta\) is the allowed displacement downwards, for example 2 mm.
  7. The cross-sections must be positive, \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} > 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\), because an area is positive. This is not a constraint \(g \le 0\), because the inequality is strict. The equilibrium constraint excludes only zero: if \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 0\), only bar \(BC\) remains and the vector \(\vek F = (0, -F)\) does not point along it, so the equation \(\mat K\vek d = \vek F\) has no solution. It does not exclude a negative cross-section, since \(\det\mat K = 0{,}36\,\tfrac{EA_{\mathrm{AC}}}{4}\,\tfrac{EA_{\mathrm{BC}}}{5}\) is nonzero also for \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} < 0\). So we demand positivity separately.

The model has idealizations, which we name because they determine where the problem holds. The displacements are small, so that equilibrium is written on the undeformed truss (the model of chapter 7, the displacement of 10,7 mm is 0,21 % of the length of bar \(BC\), which is 5 m, an estimate of the order of magnitude). The material is linearly elastic (theorem 3.11). The weight of the bars is neglected, as definition 4.4 demands: at the density of steel 7,8 Mg/m\(^3\) (BOWER, table 3.1 in §3.2.4, PDF p. 100) the two bars with a total volume of 900 cm\(^3\) have mass 7,02 kg and weight 68,9 N, which is 0,69 % of the load \(F\). The buckling of the compressed bar \(AC\) is not demanded in the problem: in the next section we shall see that this is not always justified.

The problem (29.1) is written with two kinds of unknowns, the design variables and the state, which are solved for together. For a truss, however, the state is uniquely determined for given cross-sections, so we can eliminate it.

Definition 29.2 Nested formulation (gnezdena oblika naloge)
Motivation

For every design we would first compute the state and then judge its quality. This is a computation in two layers, which we want to write down.

Let \(D \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) be the set of designs that have a meaning (for a truss, positive cross-sections), and let the matrix \(\mat K(\vek\alpha)\) be invertible for every \(\vek\alpha \in D\). For \(\vek\alpha \in D\) the state is \(\vek d(\vek\alpha) = \mat K(\vek\alpha)^{-1}\vek F\). The nested formulation (gnezdena oblika) of problem (29.1) is

\[\text{minimize } \tilde f(\vek\alpha) = f\big(\vek\alpha, \vek d(\vek\alpha)\big) \quad \text{over } \vek\alpha \in D \quad \text{subject to } \tilde g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek\alpha) = g_{\mathrm{i}}\big(\vek\alpha, \vek d(\vek\alpha)\big) \le 0 , \quad i = 1, \dots, k . \tag{29.3}\]

Problem (29.1) is the simultaneous formulation (istočasna oblika).

Explanation

The name nested is told by the layers: the state is computed inside every evaluation of the objective function and the constraints, just as an egg lies in a nest. For a truss without a mechanism the matrix \(\mat K(\vek\alpha)\) is positive definite whenever all cross-sections are positive (theorem 7.33), so for the wall truss \(D = \{A_{\mathrm{AC}} > 0,\ A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\}\). For general structures \(\tilde f\) is not necessarily a simple function.

Source: CHK §1.3 (PDF p. 14-15): simultaneous and nested formulation, \(u(x) = K(x)^{-1}F(x)\).

For the wall truss the problem can be written in the nested form with the cross-sections. We use that the forces of the bars do not depend on the cross-sections.

Derivation 29.3 Nodal displacement as a function of the areas (pomik vozlišča kot funkcija prerezov)

Goal: to express the displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) of the wall truss with the cross-sections \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), without solving a system. The assumptions are the idealizations of this section, \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\).

1
\[F\,|v_{\mathrm{C}}| = 2U = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \frac{N_{\mathrm{e}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{e}}}{E\,A_{\mathrm{e}}} .\]
Hint

By Clapeyron's theorem (theorem 4.86) the work of the load \(F\) on the displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) is twice the strain energy, and that is the sum \(\sum N_{\mathrm{e}}^2L_{\mathrm{e}}/(2EA_{\mathrm{e}})\) (equation (4.5)). The displacement downwards is \(|v_{\mathrm{C}}|\).

2
\[|v_{\mathrm{C}}| = \frac{F}{9E}\left( \frac{64}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \frac{125}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}} \right) .\]
Hint

We insert \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F\), \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F\), \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m: \(\tfrac{16}{9}F^2 \cdot 4 = \tfrac{64}{9}F^2\) and \(\tfrac{25}{9}F^2 \cdot 5 = \tfrac{125}{9}F^2\). We divide by \(F\).

Explanation

Check with cross-sections of 100 mm\(^2\) each: \(\tfrac{10^4}{9 \cdot 196\cdot 10^9}\cdot\tfrac{64 + 125}{10^{-4}}\ \text{m} = 10{,}714\) mm, as in section 7.5.2.

The function \(v_{\mathrm{C}}(A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}})\) thus exists in closed form, which is an exception: for a general structure we compute the state by computer at every design.

Source: The derivation is not from a source. Clapeyron's theorem and the energy of a bar are from chapter 4.

With the state eliminated, the constraints are functions of the cross-sections. The displacement constraint is written as \(\tfrac{F}{9E}\big(\tfrac{64}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \tfrac{125}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}}\big) \le \delta\), that is \(\tfrac{64}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \tfrac{125}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}} \le \tfrac{9E\delta}{F} = 0{,}3528\ \text{mm}^{-2}\) at \(\delta = 2\) mm. The two stress constraints are (\(N\) does not depend on the cross-sections) \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} \ge |N_{\mathrm{AC}}|/\sigma_0 = 60{,}61\) mm\(^2\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} \ge N_{\mathrm{BC}}/\sigma_0 = 75{,}76\) mm\(^2\).

But we may choose differently: the cross-section of a bar is one choice, the height of the pin \(B\) on the wall another, the decision whether a bar exists at all a third. By what the design variables describe, the problems are of three kinds.

Definition 29.4 Kinds of structural optimization (vrste optimizacije konstrukcij)
Motivation

What we change in problem (29.1) determines what kind of computation we need.

Problem (29.1) is a problem of

  1. sizing optimization (optimizacija dimenzij), if the design variables are thicknesses: areas of the cross-sections of bars or the thickness of a plate, the geometry remains,
  2. shape optimization (optimizacija oblike), if the design variables are the shape of the boundary of the body, for example the height of a pin or a curve that bounds the body. The connectivity of the body does not change, no new boundaries appear,
  3. topology optimization (topološka optimizacija), if we may reduce a thickness or an area of a cross-section to zero, and so remove parts of the structure. For a truss this means vanished bars, for a plate vanished parts of the plate.
Explanation

The name topology is of Greek origin, topos means place, and it says which parts are connected to each other. In topology optimization this connection changes, in the other two it does not.

Source: CHK §1.4 (PDF p. 15-17): sizing, shape and topology optimization, Figs. 1.2-1.5. The figures are drawn by ourselves.

The figure shows the difference. On the left the design variables are the numbers \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the geometry is given. In the middle the design variable is the height \(h\) of the pin \(B\), and since the geometry changes, the forces in the bars change too (we compute this in the next section). On the right we allowed the area of bar \(AC\) to reach \(0\). The height \(h\) is a number, but the edge of a body is a curve, a function, which has infinitely many values. If the design variable is a curve or a field, we speak of distributed parameter systems (sistemi z razporejenimi parametri), whereas for a truss there are finitely many design variables, and the system is naturally discrete (CHK §1.5, PDF p. 17). The computation is always done by computer and therefore discrete. That the solution of the discretized computation converges to the solution of the true one is usually hard to prove (CHK, PDF p. 17), so we shall describe the trust in the result for these problems separately.

Now we can write what the solutions are.

Definition 29.5 Feasible set and optimum (dopustna množica in optimum)
Motivation

All designs that meet the requirements, and among them the one with the smallest objective function.

Let the problem be in the nested form (29.3). A design \(\vek\alpha \in D\) is feasible (dopustna) if \(\tilde g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek\alpha) \le 0\) for all \(i\). The set of all feasible designs, \(\mathcal F \subseteq \mathbb R^n\), is the feasible set (dopustna množica). A design \(\vek\alpha^* \in \mathcal F\) is an optimum (optimum, the best feasible design) if \(\tilde f(\vek\alpha^*) \le \tilde f(\vek\alpha)\) for every \(\vek\alpha \in \mathcal F\). The number \(\tilde f(\vek\alpha^*)\) is the least value.

Explanation

A feasible design means an allowed one: it meets all constraints. The optimum is not necessarily unique. If two designs give the same least value, both are optima. Later we shall distinguish a local and a global minimum. Here the optimum is always the best feasible design among all.

Source: The definition is not from a source, CHK §1.3 (PDF p. 13-15) speaks of the same problem in other words.

The least value does not always exist. Two problems in which we see this are cases where one assumption is missing.

The first problem is the statement as we would write it without hesitation: the least volume of steel that still carries the load, without a stress constraint. The cross-sections must be positive, so the feasible set is the quadrant \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} > 0\), \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\) from the left half of figure 29.3.

Example 29.6 Least volume without a stress constraint

We demand only \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} > 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\). The objective function is \(f = 4A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5A_{\mathrm{BC}}\).

  1. The level lines \(f = 900\), \(450\), \(90\) are parallel and come closer to the origin with a smaller value.
  2. For the design \((A, A)\) we have \(f = 9A\) (cm\(^3\), \(A\) in mm\(^2\)): for \(A = 100\), \(10\), \(1\), \(0{,}1\) we get \(f = 900\), \(90\), \(9\), \(0{,}9\). Two points are in the figure.
  3. For every feasible design \((A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}})\) the design \((A_{\mathrm{AC}}/2, A_{\mathrm{BC}}/2)\) is feasible, since the halves are positive, and has half the value of \(f\). So no design is the best, the least value does not exist. The values are all positive and with the sequence \((1/l, 1/l)\) come arbitrarily close to \(0\), but no design reaches the value \(0\).
  4. At \(A = 0{,}1\) mm\(^2\) the stress in bar \(BC\) is \(16{,}67\ \text{kN}/0{,}1\ \text{mm}^2 = 166\,667\) MPa, which is \(758\) times the yield limit of steel (\(166\,667/220 = 757{,}6\)). The design is therefore useless, and exactly the stress constraint is missing.

The reason is that the sequence of feasible designs \((1/l, 1/l)\) converges to the origin, which is not in the set: the set is not closed (definition 1.74). When we add the stress constraints, the set in the right half of the figure closes: the edges \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 60{,}61\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 75{,}76\) are in the set.

The second problem has a closed set and still no least value. Let us take only bar \(AC\) with the force \(|N_{\mathrm{AC}}| = 13{,}33\) kN and ask how small a shortening we can find. The shortening is \(\Delta = |N_{\mathrm{AC}}|\,L_{\mathrm{AC}}/(EA_{\mathrm{AC}}) = 272{,}11\ \text{mm mm}^2/A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) (theorem 3.11, as with the shortening \(2{,}721\) mm in chapter 4 at \(100\) mm\(^2\)).

Example 29.7 Least shortening of a bar without a volume constraint

The function \(\Delta(A) = 272{,}11/A\) is continuous for \(A > 0\), the feasible set \([60{,}61, \infty)\) is closed.

  1. For the points of the curve: \(A = 60{,}61\), \(100\), \(1000\) mm\(^2\) give \(\Delta = 4{,}490\), \(2{,}721\), \(0{,}272\) mm, for \(A = 10^5\) mm\(^2\) we have \(\Delta = 0{,}0027\) mm.
  2. For every \(A\) we have \(\Delta(2A) = \tfrac12\Delta(A)\) and \(2A\) is feasible, so no design is the best. The infimum is \(0\), the curve does not reach it.
  3. The reason is that the set is not bounded: designs with \(A \to \infty\) are feasible. Without a volume constraint the "best" bar would be infinitely thick.
  4. With the volume of the bar limited to 600 cm\(^3\) we have \(A \le 150\) mm\(^2\), the set is closed and bounded, and the least shortening \(\Delta(150) = 1{,}814\) mm is at \(A = 150\) mm\(^2\) (a decreasing function reaches its least value at the right end).

The examples showed what happens if the set is not closed or not bounded. Closedness and boundedness are sufficient, as the next lemma says, which relies on the theorem on the greatest value from chapter 8.

Lemma 29.8 Existence of an optimum (obstoj optimuma)

Let the problem be in the nested form (29.3) with the feasible set \(\mathcal F \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) (definition 29.5) and let the following hold:

  1. \(\mathcal F\) is a closed set of points of the space \(\mathbb R^n\) (definition 1.74) and nonempty,
  2. \(\tilde f\) is continuous on \(\mathcal F\),
  3. for some feasible design \(\vek\alpha_0\) the set \(K = \{\vek\alpha \in \mathcal F : \tilde f(\vek\alpha) \le \tilde f(\vek\alpha_0)\}\) is bounded. This also holds when \(\mathcal F\) itself is bounded.

Then an optimum \(\vek\alpha^*\) exists.

Idea

We search for the optimum on the part of the set where closedness and boundedness are guaranteed, and use the theorem on the least value on such sets. The rest of the set cannot be better, by the definition of \(K\).

Proof

We must show that \(K\) is closed, bounded and nonempty, and that its least element is the least on the whole of \(\mathcal F\).

  1. The set \(K\) is nonempty, because it contains \(\vek\alpha_0\), and bounded by item 3.
  2. The set \(K\) is closed. Let \((\vek\alpha_{\mathrm{l}})\) be a sequence of points of \(K\) that converges to a point \(\hat{\vek\alpha}\). Since \(\mathcal F\) is closed (item 1), \(\hat{\vek\alpha} \in \mathcal F\) by definition 1.74. Since \(\tilde f\) is continuous on \(\mathcal F\), the sequence \(\tilde f(\vek\alpha_{\mathrm{l}})\) converges to \(\tilde f(\hat{\vek\alpha})\) (lemma 8.24, item 2). Since \(\tilde f(\vek\alpha_{\mathrm{l}}) \le \tilde f(\vek\alpha_0)\) for every \(l\), by lemma 1.48 also \(\tilde f(\hat{\vek\alpha}) \le \tilde f(\vek\alpha_0)\), so \(\hat{\vek\alpha} \in K\).
  3. By theorem 8.26, applied to \(K\) and \(\tilde f\), there exists \(\vek\alpha^* \in K\) with \(\tilde f(\vek\alpha^*) \le \tilde f(\vek\alpha)\) for every \(\vek\alpha \in K\).
  4. Let \(\vek\alpha \in \mathcal F\) lie outside \(K\). Then \(\tilde f(\vek\alpha) > \tilde f(\vek\alpha_0) \ge \tilde f(\vek\alpha^*)\), where the last inequality follows from step 3 with \(\vek\alpha_0 \in K\). So \(\vek\alpha^*\) is the best on the whole of \(\mathcal F\).
Explanation

If all functions \(\tilde g_{\mathrm{i}}\) are continuous on the whole space \(\mathbb R^n\), the set \(\mathcal F\) is closed by item 4 of lemma 8.24, since it is the intersection of the closed sets \(\{\tilde g_{\mathrm{i}} \le 0\}\). For a truss they are continuous only for positive cross-sections, so we ensure closedness by the two stress constraints.

Source: The proof is not from a source. CHK §1.3 (PDF p. 13-15) does not prove the existence of an optimum.

Let us test the lemma on the examples. The wall truss with the two stress constraints has \(\mathcal F = \{A_{\mathrm{AC}} \ge 60{,}61,\ A_{\mathrm{BC}} \ge 75{,}76\}\), which is a closed set, the objective function \(4A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) is continuous and \(\vek\alpha_0 = (100, 100)\) is feasible (the stresses \(133{,}3\) and \(166{,}7\) MPa are below \(220\) MPa). The set \(K\) is the triangle with vertices \((60{,}61, 75{,}76)\), \((60{,}61, 131{,}52)\) and \((130{,}30, 75{,}76)\) mm\(^2\): from \(4A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5A_{\mathrm{BC}} \le 900\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} \ge 75{,}76\) it follows that \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} \le (900 - 378{,}8)/4 = 130{,}30\), similarly \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} \le (900 - 242{,}4)/5 = 131{,}52\). It is bounded, so an optimum exists. The vertex \((60{,}61, 75{,}76)\) with volume \(621{,}2\) cm\(^3\) has the least value, as the level line \(621\) in the right figure shows, which only touches it. The proof that the optimum is exactly there follows in the next section. Without the stress constraints item 1 of the lemma is missing (example 29.6), without the volume constraint for bar \(AC\) item 3 (example 29.7).

So the wall truss has an optimum. But where is the optimum and how do we find it, when the structure has more bars or an additional constraint such as the displacement constraint? This is the topic of the rest of the chapter. The next section first finds the optimum of the wall truss with the two stress constraints, and then also the best height of the pin \(B\).

29.2 Trusses with stress constraints (paličje z napetostnimi omejitvami)

In section 7.5.2 we gave the two bars on the wall of section 4.1.4 the area \(100\ \text{mm}^2\), because it was a round number, not because anyone had chosen it. The stresses were \(-133{,}3\) and \(166{,}7\) MPa, both below the yield stress of steel, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa (chapter 3). Both bars therefore have a reserve. The question of optimization: how much steel can we save if we use up the reserve? Material is paid for by volume, so we look for the two bars of least total volume that still hold. This is a problem of definition 29.1, and in this section we solve it by hand, on a truss we know, so that we see what the general methods will later do.

29.2.1 What the bars carry

We put the truss on the board (figure 29.5, left). We draw the wall with hatching and on it the pins \(A\) and \(B\), \(B\) at \(h = 3\) m above \(A\). From \(A\) horizontally to the joint \(C\) runs bar \(AC\) with cross-section area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\), from \(B\) obliquely to \(C\) bar \(BC\) with area \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). At the joint \(C\), at distance \(a = 4\) m from the wall, hangs the load, pulling down with the force \(F = 10\) kN. Notation: \(A\) and \(B\) here are points on the wall, areas are written with an index, \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). Likewise \(C\) here is the joint, later in the chapter \(C\) will also mean compliance, and the joint will then have another name.

What the bars carry is told by the equilibrium of the joint, not by their thickness. We cut the joint \(C\) out in our mind (figure 29.5, right) and draw what acts on it. The load force \(F\) pulls down. Bar \(AC\) is compressed under the load and pushes the joint away, so its force on the joint points toward the joint along the axis of the bar and has magnitude \(|N_{\mathrm{AC}}|\). Bar \(BC\) is stretched and pulls the joint toward \(B\) along its axis, its force has magnitude \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}\). That the forces point along the bars is guaranteed by lemma 4.5 on the force in a bar of a truss. Let \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = (a, -h)/s\) be the unit vectors from the wall toward \(C\), where \(s = \sqrt{a^2 + h^2}\) is the length of bar \(BC\). The force of bar \(e\) on the joint is \(-N_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\), as in section 4.1.4. By the first condition of equilibrium (2.2) for the joint \(C\), \(-N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} + (0, -F) = \vek 0\). These are two equations,

\[N_{\mathrm{AC}} + \frac{a}{s}\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0 , \qquad -\frac{h}{s}\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -F , \tag{29.4}\]

for two unknowns. The second gives \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F\,s/h\), the first \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -F\,a/h\). At \(h = 3\) m we have \(s = 5\) m, \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN, as in section 4.1.4. No area appears in the equations. We could make the bars thinner or thicker and the equilibrium of the joint would stay the same. This property gets a name.

Definition 29.9 Statically determinate truss (statično določeno paličje)

A truss (definition 4.4) with one load case is statically determinate (statično določeno) if the equilibrium of all its free joints, written as a system of equations for the axial forces \(N_1, \dots, N_{\mathrm{n}}\) of all bars, has exactly one solution for the given forces on the joints. The axial forces are then computed from equilibrium, and contain neither the cross-section areas \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) nor the modulus of elasticity.

Source: CHK §2.1 (PDF p. 19): when the number of bars equals the number of degrees of freedom of the joint, the forces in the bars follow from the equilibrium equations alone, the truss is statically determinate. The definition is ours, in the form that lemma 29.10 needs.

Our truss is statically determinate: the matrix of system (29.4) has determinant \(1\cdot(-h/s) - (a/s)\cdot 0 = -h/s \ne 0\), so the solution is unique. This will not always be so. A truss with more bars than the joint has degrees of freedom is not statically determinate, and the forces in its bars then depend on the stiffness of the bars, that is, on the areas. We deal with it later in the chapter, in the section on least compliance.

29.2.2 The optimization problem

Let us write the problem as in definition 29.1. First the model and the idealizations, because the result holds only for them.

  • The model is the truss of section 4.1.4 with steel, \(E = 196\) GPa, density \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³. The bars have a solid round section, so each is determined by its cross-section area.
  • Idealization 1: small displacements. We compute the forces on the undeformed position. At stress \(\sigma_0\) the strain is \(\sigma_0/E = 220\ \text{MPa}/196\ \text{GPa} = 1{,}12\cdot 10^{-3}\). When we actually move the joint \(C\) (the distances from \(A\) and \(B\) change by this fraction, the joint is found by Newton's method in NumPy) and compute the equilibrium of the joint once more on the deformed position, the forces change by \(0{,}11\) %. The source of this number is the computation in num-02.py.
  • Idealization 2: allowed stress \(\sigma_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa in tension and compression, with no safety factor. A factor would multiply all areas by the same number, as we shall see from equation (29.7).
  • Idealization 3: the weight of the bars is neglected. At the areas we find in this section the two bars weigh \(47{,}5\) N together against \(10\) kN, that is \(0{,}48\) %. Lemma 4.5 would then not hold exactly, since weight acts between the joints.
  • Idealization 4: areas are arbitrary positive numbers. Real bars have sections from a catalogue.

The design variables (projektni spremenljivki) are the areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). The objective function (ciljna funkcija) is the volume of material,

\[V(A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}}) = L_{\mathrm{AC}}\,A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}\,A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 4\,A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5\,A_{\mathrm{BC}} \quad (\text{m}\cdot\text{mm}^2 = \text{cm}^3) , \tag{29.5}\]

because a straight bar with cross-section area \(A\) and length \(L\) contains \(A\,L\) of material (area times length), and because \(1\ \text{mm}^2\cdot 1\ \text{m} = 1000\ \text{mm}^3 = 1\ \text{cm}^3\). We use volume instead of weight. The weight is \(\rho\,g\,V\) with the same density \(\rho\) in both bars, so it is proportional to the volume, and both are smallest at the same areas. (The letter \(g\) elsewhere in the book means the acceleration of gravity. Here we write it for the acceleration only in this remark, otherwise it denotes constraints, \(g_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{BC}}\).)

The stress constraint (omejitev napetosti) demands that the stress in each bar, by definition 2.6, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{e}} = N_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\), not exceed the allowed one in absolute value,

\[g_{\mathrm{e}}(A_{\mathrm{e}}) = \frac{|N_{\mathrm{e}}|}{A_{\mathrm{e}}} - \sigma_0 \le 0 , \qquad e \in \{AC, BC\} . \tag{29.6}\]

By static determinacy, \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) are numbers, not functions of the areas. Since \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\), multiplying the inequality by \(A_{\mathrm{e}}/\sigma_0 > 0\) does not reverse its direction and gives \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge |N_{\mathrm{e}}|/\sigma_0\). So only lower bounds on the areas remain, not two curves (figure 29.6). On the figure the axes carry the areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) in mm². The feasible set (definition 29.5) is a corner, bounded by the vertical line at \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 13\,333/220 = 60{,}61\ \text{mm}^2\) and the horizontal at \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16\,667/220 = 75{,}76\ \text{mm}^2\), and it extends without limit upward and to the right. There is no bound above, since a thicker bar still holds, and is only dearer.

Where in it is the least volume? Equation (29.5) is linear, so the points of equal volume are straight lines, the level lines of the objective. For \(V = 400\ \text{cm}^3\) (dashed) the line lies entirely below the feasible set, no section of this volume holds. For \(V = 621{,}2\ \text{cm}^3\) the line just touches the feasible set at the corner. For \(V = 900\ \text{cm}^3\) it cuts it, and on it lies our first choice, \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 100\ \text{mm}^2\), which is inside the set. Any move from this choice toward smaller areas is a saving, until we hit one of the bounds. The same reasoning holds for every truss of this kind, so we prove it.

Lemma 29.10 The fully stressed truss is optimal (polno napeto paličje je optimalno)

Let the truss be statically determinate (definition 29.9) with \(n\) bars of lengths \(L_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) and axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}} \ne 0\), and let \(\sigma_0 > 0\). Among all areas \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\) that satisfy \(|N_{\mathrm{e}}|/A_{\mathrm{e}} \le \sigma_0\) for all \(e\), the volume \(V = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\) has exactly one least value, at

\[A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*} = \frac{|N_{\mathrm{e}}|}{\sigma_0} , \quad e = 1, \dots, n , \tag{29.7}\]

and the stress in every bar is then exactly \(\sigma_0\) in absolute value.

Proof

We must show that the volume has its least value on the feasible set at \(A^*\) and nowhere else.

  1. Since \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) are numbers independent of the areas (definition 29.9), \(|N_{\mathrm{e}}|/A_{\mathrm{e}} \le \sigma_0\) with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) is equivalent to \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge |N_{\mathrm{e}}|/\sigma_0 = A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*}\), because we multiply by \(A_{\mathrm{e}}/\sigma_0 > 0\). The feasible set is therefore \(\{A : A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*}\ \forall e\}\), the lower bounds of different bars do not influence each other.
  2. Let \(A\) be feasible. Then \(V(A) - V(A^{*}) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*})\), and every term is nonnegative, since \(L_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*} \ge 0\) by step 1.
  3. A sum of nonnegative terms is zero exactly when every term is zero, so \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*}\) for every \(e\), since \(L_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). The point \(A^{*}\) is feasible and is the only least one.
  4. The stress at \(A^{*}\) is \(N_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^{*} = \sigma_0\,N_{\mathrm{e}}/|N_{\mathrm{e}}| = \pm\sigma_0\).

Source: CHK §2.1 (PDF pp. 18 to 21) solves the same kind of problem for a truss of two stretched bars of equal length graphically as a linear program in two variables (figure 2.3, PDF p. 20) and finds that at the optimum the stress in both bars is at its upper bound (PDF p. 21). The proof is not from the source.

The lemma says that the problem is trivial once the forces are known: each bar gets the least area that still holds its stress. CHK notes that such a linear structure is rare and depends on the truss being statically determinate and the constraints being simple (§2.1, PDF p. 20). The requirement \(N_{\mathrm{e}} \ne 0\) is a condition of the lemma: a bar with \(N_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) would have least area zero, and the requirement \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) does not let a least value be found, since the infimum zero would not be reached. The bar disappears from the structure, which is a topology change (CHK §2.1, PDF p. 21), and with the vanished bar the truss changes. What this does to equilibrium we shall see in the section on least compliance.

Example 29.11 The fully stressed wall truss (polno napeto paličje na steni)

Equation (29.7) gives at \(h = 3\) m, \(F = 10\) kN and \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa

\[A_{\mathrm{AC}}^{*} = \frac{13\,333{,}3\ \text{N}}{220\ \text{N/mm}^2} = 60{,}61\ \text{mm}^2 , \qquad A_{\mathrm{BC}}^{*} = \frac{16\,666{,}7\ \text{N}}{220\ \text{N/mm}^2} = 75{,}76\ \text{mm}^2 .\]

By equation (29.5), \(V = 4\cdot 60{,}61 + 5\cdot 75{,}76 = 621{,}2\ \text{cm}^3\), mass \(\rho V = 4{,}845\) kg. The first choice with \(100\ \text{mm}^2\) had \(900\ \text{cm}^3\). We saved \((900 - 621{,}2)/900 = 31\) % of the material, and the stresses in the bars are now \(-220\) and \(220\) MPa instead of \(-133{,}3\) and \(166{,}7\) MPa (NumPy, num-02.py).

Back to the assumption of static determinacy: without it step 1 of the proof fails, because the forces are functions of the areas and the constraints are no longer an upper or lower bound on one variable. The first example of such a problem is in the section on least compliance, later in the chapter.

29.2.3 The best height of the joint

So far we have held \(B\) at \(h = 3\) m. Nobody prescribes the position of the pin on the wall, and the height is one more design variable. Since it changes the shape of the truss and not only the thicknesses, it is a shape variable (see definition 29.4 on the kinds of optimization). At each height we can use lemma 29.10, so the least volume at that height is a function of one variable, \(V(h)\). Which height reduces it most? We expect two opposing effects. A flat truss (small \(h\)) has by equation (29.4) large forces, \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F\,s/h\) and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -F\,a/h\), which grow as \(h\) falls, so they need thick bars. A steep truss (large \(h\)) has small forces, but a longer bar \(BC\) with \(s = \sqrt{a^2 + h^2}\). The best height is somewhere in between (figure 29.7).

Lemma 29.12 Best height of the joint (najboljša višina vozlišča)

Let the pin \(A\) be on the wall at \((-a, 0)\), the pin \(B\) at \((-a, h)\) with \(h > 0\), the joint \(C\) at \((0, 0)\) with a vertical load \(F > 0\), and let \(\sigma_0 > 0\). The volume of the fully stressed truss is

\[V(h) = \frac{F\,(2a^2 + h^2)}{h\,\sigma_0} = \frac{F}{\sigma_0}\Big(h + \frac{2a^2}{h}\Big) , \tag{29.8}\]

and on \(h \in (0, \infty)\) it has exactly one least value, at \(h = a\sqrt{2}\), equal to \(V = 2\sqrt{2}\,F\,a/\sigma_0\). The least volume over all areas and heights is this value.

Proof

We must show the form of equation (29.8) and that \(h = a\sqrt2\) attains the least value.

  1. By equation (29.4), \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -F\,a/h\) and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F\,s/h\), both nonzero. By lemma 29.10 the least volume at the given height is at \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = F\,a/(h\,\sigma_0)\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = F\,s/(h\,\sigma_0)\).
  2. The bars have lengths \(a\) and \(s\), so \(V(h) = a\cdot\dfrac{F\,a}{h\,\sigma_0} + s\cdot\dfrac{F\,s}{h\,\sigma_0} = \dfrac{F\,(a^2 + s^2)}{h\,\sigma_0}\). With \(s^2 = a^2 + h^2\) this is equation (29.8).
  3. For every \(h > 0\) we have \(h + \dfrac{2a^2}{h} - 2\sqrt2\,a = \dfrac{(h - \sqrt2\,a)^2}{h}\), which we see by multiplying out: \((h - \sqrt2 a)^2 = h^2 - 2\sqrt2 a h + 2a^2\), divided by \(h\).
  4. The right side is \(\ge 0\) and equals zero exactly at \(h = \sqrt2\,a\). So \(V(h) \ge \dfrac{F}{\sigma_0}\,2\sqrt2\,a\) with equality only at \(h = a\sqrt2\).
  5. Every choice \((h, A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}})\) with feasible areas has by lemma 29.10 volume at least \(V(h)\), so by step 4 at least \(2\sqrt2\,F a/\sigma_0\), and this value is attained (figure 29.7, the lowest point).

Source: CHK in the introduction of chapter 2 (PDF p. 18) mentions that an example of combined shape and sizing optimization of a two-bar truss is in exercise 2.5. We did not read the exercise. The variable \(h\), the proof and equation (29.8) are not from the source.

Step 3 can also be said in words: the product \(h\cdot(2a^2/h) = 2a^2\) does not depend on \(h\), and a sum of two positive numbers with a given product is smallest when the numbers are equal, that is, \(h = 2a^2/h\). The term \(2a^2/h\) is the "price of the forces" (large forces at small \(h\)), the term \(h\) is the "price of the length" (a long bar \(BC\) at large \(h\)). With our numbers \(F a/\sigma_0 = 181{,}8\ \text{cm}^3\) and the best height is \(h = 4\sqrt2 = 5{,}657\) m, which corresponds to the angle \(\arctan\sqrt2 = 54{,}74^\circ\) between \(BC\) and \(AC\). There \(V = 2\sqrt2\cdot 181{,}8 = 514{,}3\ \text{cm}^3\), and the areas are \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 32{,}14\ \text{mm}^2\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 55{,}67\ \text{mm}^2\). Figure 29.7 shows it. The axes carry the height \(h\) and the volume \(V\). The curve \(V(h)\) falls from the left. The point at \(h = 1{,}5\) m is at \(1037{,}9\ \text{cm}^3\), the point at \(3\) m at \(621{,}2\ \text{cm}^3\), the lowest point is at \(h = a\sqrt2\), which the dashed guides point to, and the point at \(8\) m is higher again, at \(545{,}5\ \text{cm}^3\). Below the curve are the trusses for three heights, with line widths proportional to the areas. At \(h = 1{,}5\) m both bars are thick, at \(h = 3\) m thinner, at \(h = 5{,}657\) m thinnest, but longer.

Example 29.13 Heights of the wall truss (višine paličja na steni)

The table (NumPy, num-02.py) has the same points as figure 29.7, for \(a = 4\) m, \(F = 10\) kN, \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa:

\(h\) (m) \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) (\(\text{mm}^2\)) \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) (\(\text{mm}^2\)) \(V\) (\(\text{cm}^3\)) \(V/(F a/\sigma_0)\)
1,5 121,21 129,45 1037,9 5,708
3 60,61 75,76 621,2 3,417
5,657 32,14 55,67 514,3 2,828
8 22,73 50,82 545,5 3,000

Shorter bars are not lighter (figure 29.7, the left truss): \(h = 1{,}5\) m gives \(1{,}67\) times as much material as \(h = 3\) m, because both forces are larger at \(h = 1{,}5\) m, \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -26{,}67\) kN twice and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 28{,}48\) kN \(1{,}71\) times. At \(h = 8\) m there is again more material than at \(5{,}657\) m (\(545{,}5\) against \(514{,}3\ \text{cm}^3\)), because bar \(BC\) is \(8{,}94\) m long. The derivative \(V'(h) = (F/\sigma_0)(1 - 2a^2/h^2)\) equals \(-116{,}2\ \text{cm}^3/\text{m}\) at \(h = 3\) m, so at this height raising the pin \(B\) still helps, and at \(5{,}657\) m it is zero.

29.2.4 When fully stressed is not enough

Lemma 29.10 has a condition that is easy to overlook: the only constraints are stress constraints (figure 29.8 shows what happens when this fails). Let us see what happens if we add one that is always present in mechanics, for a compressed bar. Bar \(AC\) is in compression, and a compressed bar can lose stability: the straight position is still an equilibrium, but no longer stable, and the bar bows out sideways (buckling, uklon). By theorem 8.134 the second variation of the potential energy is positive exactly for \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/L^2\), for a bar with pinned ends, of length \(L\), with bending stiffness \(EI\). A bar with pins at the ends corresponds to the model we have.

Take a solid round section of diameter \(d\) (figure 29.8, section at the top). From \(A = \pi d^2/4\) follows \(d^2 = 4A/\pi\) and \(I = \pi d^4/64 = A^2/(4\pi)\). The critical force is by theorem 8.134

\[P_{\mathrm{cr}}(A) = \frac{\pi^2 E}{L^2}\cdot\frac{A^2}{4\pi} = \frac{\pi E A^2}{4 L^2} . \tag{29.9}\]

The fully stressed bar \(AC\) at \(h = 3\) m has \(A = 60{,}61\ \text{mm}^2\), \(d = 8{,}78\) mm and \(L = 4\) m. Its critical force is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 35{,}34\) N, and it is loaded with \(13\,333\) N, \(377\) times more (figure 29.8). The thin bar with the section of diameter 8,78 mm, at the top of the figure, would bow out under the force \(|N_{\mathrm{AC}}|\), and the bow is drawn strongly exaggerated. Both bars in the figure have the same length \(L\). The stress constraint is satisfied here with equality, but the bar does not fail because the material would exceed its limit, it fails because it loses stability, and the stress says nothing about that.

So let us add a second constraint, which the thick bar at the bottom of figure 29.8 satisfies, \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}(A_{\mathrm{AC}}) \ge |N_{\mathrm{AC}}|\) (with no safety factor, as for stress). By equation (29.9) this is \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}^2 \ge 4L^2|N_{\mathrm{AC}}|/(\pi E)\), so

\[A_{\mathrm{AC}} \ge 2L\sqrt{\frac{|N_{\mathrm{AC}}|}{\pi E}} = 8\ \text{m}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{13\,333\ \text{N}}{\pi\cdot 196\cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}}} = 1177\ \text{mm}^2 . \tag{29.10}\]

The constraint is nonlinear in \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\), but still a lower bound on one variable, because \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) does not depend on the areas. The proof of lemma 29.10 therefore still holds, if for the lower bound of bar \(AC\) we take the larger of the two bounds, \(60{,}61\ \text{mm}^2\) from stress and \(1177\ \text{mm}^2\) from equation (29.10). The larger one is the buckling bound.

Example 29.14 Buckling defeats the fully stressed truss (uklon premaga polno napeto paličje)

With the bound (29.10) we have \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1177{,}2\ \text{mm}^2\), \(d = 38{,}72\) mm (figure 29.8, the thick bar and its section at the bottom, drawn to the same scale as the thin one). The stress is \(13\,333/1177{,}2 = 11{,}33\) MPa, which is about a twentieth of the allowed one. The volume is \(4\cdot 1177{,}2 + 5\cdot 75{,}76 = 5087{,}7\ \text{cm}^3\), \(8{,}2\) times as much as \(621{,}2\ \text{cm}^3\), and the mass is \(39{,}7\) kg. Bar \(BC\) is in tension and does not lose stability, it stays at \(75{,}76\ \text{mm}^2\).

The conclusion (figure 29.8, the thick bar has a stress far below the allowed one) we shall need in the following sections: the fully stressed truss is not optimal in general, only when all constraints are stress constraints. When a constraint arrives that is below the allowed stress (buckling, displacement, natural frequency), the optimal bar sits at the bound of that constraint, and its stress is below the allowed one. Lemma 29.10 stays in the form "each constraint is a lower bound on one area, so each bar gets the largest of the bounds". This no longer holds when a constraint involves several areas at once or when the forces are not independent of the areas. Such constraints (displacement of the joint) will come up in the following sections of the chapter.

Buckling also changes the best height of figure 29.7, where the lowest point would no longer hold. With the bound (29.10) at every height, the least volume over the height has its minimum at \(h = 20{,}56\) m with \(V = 2768{,}6\ \text{cm}^3\) (NumPy, grid search from 0,5 to 200 m, num-02.py), and no longer at \(5{,}657\) m. Such a height next to a \(4\) m long horizontal bar is not sensible, so the problem would need a geometry constraint as well (the wall is not higher than a few metres). Nor can the weight be neglected as lightly any more: at \(h = 3\) m with the buckling bound the two bars weigh \(389\) N, that is \(3{,}9\) % of \(F\) instead of \(0{,}48\) %. We also chose a solid round section because of \(I = A^2/(4\pi)\). A tube would have a larger \(I\) at the same area, so it would resist buckling with a smaller area and a smaller volume, but that is a problem with two variables per section (CHK §2.2, PDF pp. 21 to 23 uses a round section as we do, and finds that, depending on the coefficients, the stress or the buckling constraint is active, PDF p. 22).

29.2.5 What we have learned

On the truss of chapters 4 and 7 we derived three things. First, for a statically determinate truss with stress constraints the least volume is at the fully stressed truss (lemma 29.10), \(621{,}2\ \text{cm}^3\) instead of \(900\ \text{cm}^3\). Second, the height of the joint is a shape variable with the best value \(a\sqrt2\) and \(514{,}3\ \text{cm}^3\) (lemma 29.12). Third, when a constraint arrives that is not a stress constraint, fully stressed is no longer optimal, buckling at \(h = 3\) m demands \(8{,}2\) times as much material. On the same truss we shall try, in the following sections of the chapter, general methods that do not require static determinacy, among others for a constraint on the displacement of the joint, which depends on both areas at once and for which the fully stressed truss does not help.

29.3 Convexity and the global minimum (konveksnost in globalni najmanjši)

For the wall truss we chose the height \(h\) where the derivative of the volume is zero (section 29.2). Is this really the least volume among all heights, or only the least nearby? Every computer procedure for finding a least value asks the same question: it takes steps downhill and stops when no small step lowers the objective function. It therefore stops at a point that is best in its neighbourhood, while we want to know that it is best among all admissible designs. This section answers when the two statements are the same. First we name both kinds of least value, then we introduce convexity, a property of sets and functions that makes them equal, and then we look for tests by which convexity is recognized on a structure.

29.3.1 Local and global minima (lokalni in globalni najmanjši)

We first see everything on a function of one variable. We take the artificial function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + 0{,}4\,x\), which comes from no structure and is chosen only so that it has all kinds of points at once. The feasible set (definition 29.5) is the interval \(S = [-1{,}4;\ 1{,}4]\), and in figure 29.9 we draw it as the thick line under the graph. Above it is the graph of the function \(f\), since the objective function (definition 29.1) is a rule that assigns a number to every design from \(S\). Three points on the graph differ in what happens in them. At \(x_1 = -1{,}0467\) the function has the value \(-0{,}4095\), the lowest on the whole interval. At \(x_3 = 0{,}9456\) it has the value \(0{,}3894\), which is higher than \(f(x_1)\) but lower than all values in the neighbourhood of radius \(r\), drawn below as a segment of length \(2r\) around \(x_3\). At \(x_2 = 0{,}1010\) the function has a peak with the value \(1{,}0201\). In all three points the tangent is horizontal, that is, the derivative is zero, and in the figure they appear as two bottoms and a peak.

The words we will use from now on are thus exact. A point at which the gradient of the function is zero is called stationary (stacionarna), because the graph is at rest there to first order: the tangent (for several coordinates the tangent plane) is horizontal. For \(n\) coordinates the gradient \(\nabla f\) is the column of partial derivatives (definition 8.22, item 3). In figure 29.9, \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) are stationary points, but only \(x_1\) and \(x_3\) are minima.

Definition 29.15 Local and global minimum (lokalni in globalni najmanjši)

Let \(S\) be a nonempty set of points with \(n\) coordinates (definition 8.22) and \(f\) a function that assigns a number to every point of \(S\). A point \(\vek x^* \in S\) is a global minimum (globalni najmanjši) of the function \(f\) on \(S\) if

\[f(\vek x^*) \le f(\vek x) \quad \text{for every point } \vek x \in S . \tag{29.11}\]

A point \(\vek x^* \in S\) is a local minimum (lokalni najmanjši) of the function \(f\) on \(S\) if there is a number \(r > 0\) such that \(f(\vek x^*) \le f(\vek x)\) for every point \(\vek x \in S\) with \(|\vek x - \vek x^*| < r\). Every global minimum is also a local one.

Source: CHK §3.1 (PDF p. 45): "global minimum" and "local minimum", "any global minimum is also a local minimum".

The name local says that we compare the value only with values nearby, in the neighbourhood of the point, and the name global that we compare it with the values on the whole set \(S\). In the figure \(x_1\) and \(x_3\) are local minima, only \(x_1\) is global. A computer procedure that starts at \(x = 1{,}2\) and goes downhill stops at \(x_3\) and reports the value \(0{,}3894\), although \(-0{,}4095\) is possible. The procedure thus misses by \(0{,}3894 - (-0{,}4095) = 0{,}7989\). For a structure this means a heavier structure than needed, and the procedure would not notice. What must hold for \(f\) and \(S\) so that this cannot happen?

29.3.2 Convex set and convex function (konveksna množica in konveksna funkcija)

Let us see why it happened. Between \(x_3\) and \(x_1\) lies the peak \(x_2\). A procedure that stops at \(x_3\) would have to cross the peak, where the function is higher, to reach the lower point, and nothing in the neighbourhood of \(x_3\) hints at this. The peak means that above the intermediate point the graph lies above the segment connecting the points on the graph at \(x_1\) and \(x_3\): the segment runs between the values \(-0{,}4095\) and \(0{,}3894\), while the graph at \(x_2\) is at \(1{,}0201\). A function for which this cannot happen has its graph below every such segment. So this segment becomes the measure.

We begin with sets, because the set in which we move must be such that we can go from one point to another along a straight line without leaving the admissible designs. We draw it in figure 29.10. The blue boundary on the left bounds a set in the plane. In it we put the points \(\vek x\) and \(\vek y\) and connect them by a segment. The points of the segment are \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\) for a number \(t\) between \(0\) and \(1\), which is the point \(\vek x\) at \(t = 0\), the point \(\vek y\) at \(t = 1\), and at \(t = 0{,}4\) the point \(\vek z\) that is \(0{,}4\) of the whole way from \(\vek x\) toward \(\vek y\) (orange in the figure). The whole segment lies in the set. On the right the boundary of the set goes around a notch. In this set too we put points \(\vek x\) and \(\vek y\) and connect them by a segment, but its midpoint \(\vek z\) lies in the notch, outside the set, as the empty circle shows. Such a set is called nonconvex.

Definition 29.16 Convex set (konveksna množica)

A set \(S\) of points with \(n\) coordinates is convex (konveksna) if for every two points \(\vek x, \vek y \in S\) and every number \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\) we have \((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y \in S\).

Source: CHK §3.2 (PDF p. 46). The same notion as the convex set in definition 4.103 (LEBL2 §8.1.4, PDF p. 16), except that there it is written with the segment from a chosen point.

The name convex comes from the Latin word convexus, bulging: a convex set has no notch, it bulges outward everywhere. The empty set is convex, because it has no points for which the condition would have to be checked. A set with one point \(\vek x\) is convex, because \((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek x = \vek x\). The quadrant \(\{A_1 \ge 0,\ A_2 \ge 0\}\) is also convex: the coordinates of a point on the segment are \((1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{i}} + t\,y_{\mathrm{i}}\), a sum of two nonnegative numbers. An open interval on a line, such as \(\{h > 0\}\) of example 29.23, is convex too.

Now functions. For the wall truss we are interested in the volume as a function of the height, and for it we will see that the graph never goes above the segment between two of its points. Figure 29.11 on the left shows this on the function \(V(h) = F\,(2a^2 + h^2)/(h\,\sigma_0)\) of section 29.2, where \(a = 4\) m is the horizontal distance of the joint \(\mathrm{B}\) from \(\mathrm{C}\), \(F = 10\) kN and \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa. We divide the volume by the unit \(F a/\sigma_0 = 181{,}82\) cm\(^3\), so that \(V/(F a/\sigma_0) = (32 + h^2)/(4h)\) with \(h\) in metres. We draw the blue graph between \(h = 1{,}2\) m and \(h = 8{,}2\) m, above the axes for \(h\) and \(V\). We choose the points \(P\) and \(Q\) on the graph at \(h_1 = 1{,}5\) m and \(h_2 = 8\) m, where \(V/(F a/\sigma_0)\) equals \(5{,}7083\) and \(3{,}0000\), and connect them by a segment that we call the chord (tetiva). At the midpoint \(\bar h = 4{,}75\) m the point \(R\) on the chord is at \(4{,}3542\) and the point \(T\) on the graph at \(2{,}8717\). The graph is below the chord here: \(T\) is below \(R\) by \(1{,}4825\) units.

Definition 29.17 Convex function (konveksna funkcija)

Let \(S\) be a convex set (definition 29.16) and \(f\) a function that assigns a number to every point of \(S\). The function \(f\) is convex (konveksna) on \(S\) if for every two points \(\vek x, \vek y \in S\) and every number \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\)

\[f\big((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\big) \le (1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) . \tag{29.12}\]

The function \(f\) is strictly convex (strogo konveksna) on \(S\) if in (29.12) the strict inequality \(<\) holds for \(\vek x \ne \vek y\) and \(0 < t < 1\).

Source: CHK §3.2 (PDF p. 46). For a functional the same property is introduced in chapter 5 (theorem 5.73).

The right side of inequality (29.12) is the value of the chord at \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\): at \(t = 0\) it is \(f(\vek x)\), at \(t = 1\) it is \(f(\vek y)\), and in between it changes linearly with \(t\). The left side is the value of the graph. In the figure \(t = (4{,}75 - 1{,}5)/(8 - 1{,}5) = 0{,}5\), the right side is \(0{,}5 \cdot 5{,}7083 + 0{,}5 \cdot 3{,}0000 = 4{,}3542\) and the left \(2{,}8717\), which the point \(T\) below the point \(R\) tells. The inequality holds here for one pair of points and one \(t\). Convexity requires that it holds for every pair and every \(t\), so one pair does not let us claim that \(V\) is convex. We check this in example 29.23.

The name convex function has the same reason as the name of a set. The set of points \((\vek x, s)\) with \(s \ge f(\vek x)\), that is, everything above the graph, is convex: if \(s \ge f(\vek x)\) and \(w \ge f(\vek y)\), then \((1 - t)\,s + t\,w \ge (1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) \ge f\big((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\big)\), the last inequality being (29.12), and the point \(\big((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y,\ (1 - t)\,s + t\,w\big)\) is again above the graph. For strict convexity the inequality is strict and the graph contains no segment.

29.3.3 Why convexity guarantees a global minimum (zakaj konveksnost zagotavlja globalni najmanjši)

Now we can answer the question from the beginning of the section. The procedure stops at a local minimum \(\vek x^*\) (figure 29.9, point \(x_3\)), so in the ball of radius \(r\) around it there is no lower value. Suppose that somewhere in \(S\) there were a point \(\vek y\) with a lower value. The chord from \(\vek x^*\) to \(\vek y\) (like \(PQ\) in figure 29.11) starts at \(f(\vek x^*)\) and falls to \(f(\vek y)\), and convexity says that the graph is below it. Already near \(\vek x^*\) the chord is below \(f(\vek x^*)\), so the graph is below it there too, in the ball with a lower value, which a local minimum forbids.

Lemma 29.18 A local minimum of a convex function is global (lokalni najmanjši konveksne funkcije je globalni)

Let \(S\) be a nonempty convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(f\) a convex function on \(S\).

  1. Every local minimum of \(f\) on \(S\) is a global minimum.
  2. The set of points at which \(f\) attains a global minimum is convex.
  3. If \(f\) is strictly convex, there is at most one such point.
Proof

We must show the first part by contradiction, then the other two work with the same chord. We need the convexity of \(S\) so that the points on the segment stay in \(S\), and the convexity of the function so that the value on the segment lies below the chord.

  1. Let \(\vek x^*\) be a local minimum with radius \(r\) (definition 29.15) and let there be \(\vek y \in S\) with \(f(\vek y) < f(\vek x^*)\). Then \(\vek y \ne \vek x^*\).
  2. For \(0 < t \le 1\) the point \(\vek z_{\mathrm{t}} = (1 - t)\,\vek x^* + t\,\vek y\) is in \(S\), because \(S\) is convex (definition 29.16).
  3. The difference is \(\vek z_{\mathrm{t}} - \vek x^* = t\,(\vek y - \vek x^*)\) and by item 3 of lemma 8.23 its length is \(t\,|\vek y - \vek x^*|\). We choose \(t\) with \(0 < t < 1\) and \(t\,|\vek y - \vek x^*| < r\). Then \(\vek z_{\mathrm{t}}\) is in the ball of radius \(r\) around \(\vek x^*\).
  4. By convexity (29.12), \(f(\vek z_{\mathrm{t}}) \le (1 - t)\,f(\vek x^*) + t\,f(\vek y) = f(\vek x^*) + t\,\big(f(\vek y) - f(\vek x^*)\big)\). Since \(t > 0\) and \(f(\vek y) - f(\vek x^*) < 0\), we have \(f(\vek z_{\mathrm{t}}) < f(\vek x^*)\).
  5. The point \(\vek z_{\mathrm{t}}\) is in \(S\) and in the ball of radius \(r\), and its value is lower than \(f(\vek x^*)\). This contradicts the local minimum. Hence \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x^*)\) for every \(\vek y \in S\) and \(\vek x^*\) is a global minimum.
  6. Second part: let \(\vek x^*\) and \(\vek y^*\) be global minima with the value \(m\) and \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x^* + t\,\vek y^*\). The point \(\vek z\) is in \(S\), so \(f(\vek z) \ge m\), and by (29.12) \(f(\vek z) \le (1 - t)\,m + t\,m = m\). Hence \(f(\vek z) = m\) and \(\vek z\) is again a global minimum.
  7. Third part: if \(\vek x^* \ne \vek y^*\) and \(f\) is strictly convex, then at \(t = \tfrac12\) item 6 gives with a strict inequality \(f(\vek z) < m\). This contradicts \(m\) being the least value.

Source: CHK §3.2 (PDF p. 47) states the claims without proof: "local minima are also global minima for convex problems" and "if the objective function is strictly convex and the feasible set is convex, there exists at most one solution". The proof is not from the source.

The proof showed that for a convex function on a convex set (as in figure 29.11) a local minimum cannot have a lower point anywhere, and that all minima are equally high and form a convex set. The proof does not say that a minimum exists. The function \(1/x\) is strictly convex on the closed but unbounded convex set \(x \ge 1\), its values fall toward \(0\), which it attains nowhere (CHK, PDF p. 47). For a closed and bounded feasible set and a continuous objective function existence is guaranteed by lemma 29.8, and convexity is not needed for it (CHK, PDF p. 47).

Two requirements of the lemma remain, each with its own example showing that it is not superfluous: a convex function and a convex set. Figure 29.9 is the first example: the function is nonconvex, and indeed it has two local minima. The second example is the conditions that the structure itself sets.

Example 29.19 Two parallel bars, each removed or at least 40 mm² (dve vzporedni palici, vsaka odstranjena ali vsaj 40 mm²)

Two bars of length \(L = 1\) m connect the same two joints: the first is fixed, the second is pulled by the force \(F = 10\) kN along both bars. The first bar is steel with \(E_1 = 196\) GPa, the second an aluminium alloy with \(E_2 = 74\) GPa (the middle of the range in the table of section 3.1.2), their cross-sections are \(A_1\) and \(A_2\). The elongation \(\Delta\) is the same for both bars, since they connect the same joints, and the axial forces are \(N_{\mathrm{i}} = E_{\mathrm{i}} A_{\mathrm{i}} \Delta/L\) by Hooke's law (theorem 3.11). The equilibrium of the joint is \(F = N_1 + N_2 = (E_1 A_1 + E_2 A_2)\,\Delta/L\). Let the elongation be at most \(1\) mm. The condition is \(\Delta = F L/(E_1 A_1 + E_2 A_2) \le 1\) mm, that is,

\[196\,A_1 + 74\,A_2 \ge 10\,000 \qquad (A_1, A_2 \text{ in mm}^2, \text{ which with the moduli in GPa gives the force in kN}) . \tag{29.13}\]

The volume is \(V = (A_1 + A_2)\,L\) and we reduce it. We add a condition that the manufacturer makes no bars thinner than \(40\) mm\(^2\): each bar is removed (\(A_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\)) or has \(A_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 40\) mm\(^2\). This is a simple form of a topology choice: a bar is either there or it is not.

In figure 29.12 we draw every design as a point of the plane \((A_1, A_2)\). Because of the condition \(A_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) or \(A_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 40\) the feasible set has fallen apart into three pieces. On the left is the line \(A_1 = 0\) with \(A_2 \ge 40\), below the line \(A_2 = 0\) with \(A_1 \ge 40\) and at the top right the quadrant with \(A_1, A_2 \ge 40\) (hatched). The orange segment is the equality in (29.13) from \((51{,}02;\ 0)\) to \((0;\ 135{,}14)\), only the points on its upper right side are admissible, where the left side of (29.13) is larger. Condition (29.13) is linear, so each of the three pieces is convex, and on each we find the least volume separately. On the lower piece, \(A_2 = 0\), we need \(196\,A_1 \ge 10\,000\), so the best is \(A_1 = 51{,}02\) mm\(^2\) and \(V = 51{,}02\) cm\(^3\). On the left piece, \(A_1 = 0\), we have \(A_2 = 10\,000/74 = 135{,}14\) mm\(^2\) and \(V = 135{,}14\) cm\(^3\). On the quadrant condition (29.13) at \(A_1 = A_2 = 40\) is satisfied with a reserve (\(196 \cdot 40 + 74 \cdot 40 = 10\,800 \ge 10\,000\)), so the best is simply the lower left corner, \(V = 80\) cm\(^3\).

All three points \(S_1\), \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) are local minima. Take \(r = 30\) mm\(^2\). Points from different pieces differ in at least one of the areas by at least \(40\) mm\(^2\) (one area is zero, the other at least \(40\)), so they are farther apart than \(r\) and the ball of radius \(r\) contains points of only one piece. Around \(S_1 = (51{,}02;\ 0)\) only the points \((A_1, 0)\) are therefore admissible, and by (29.13) \(A_1 \ge 51{,}02\) and \(V \ge 51{,}02\) cm\(^3\) there. Likewise around \(S_3\): only \((0, A_2)\) with \(A_2 \ge 135{,}14\) are admissible. Around \(S_2 = (40;\ 40)\) only the points with \(A_1 \ge 40\) and \(A_2 \ge 40\) are admissible, so \(V \ge 80\) cm\(^3\). A procedure that starts at a large aluminium bar stops at \(S_3\) with \(135{,}14\) cm\(^3\), which is \(2{,}65\) times more than the global minimum \(51{,}02\) cm\(^3\). Lemma 29.18 therefore does not apply, since the set is nonconvex: the midpoint of the segment between \(S_1\) and \(S_3\) is \((25{,}51;\ 67{,}57)\) and satisfies condition (29.13) with equality, but has \(A_1 = 25{,}51\), which is neither zero nor at least \(40\), and is therefore not admissible (empty circle). If we replace the condition \(A_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) or \(A_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 40\) by \(A_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\), then \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) are no longer local minima: along the line (29.13) we have \(V = 135{,}14 - 1{,}6486\,A_1\) (NumPy), which falls down to \(S_1\), and \(S_1\) remains the only local, hence global, minimum.

The example shows that the convexity of the set is not a formality. For a truss with removable bars the local solutions differ by more than a factor of two (\(S_1\) against \(S_3\)), and a procedure that stops at a local minimum cannot know that a better one exists. Lemma 29.18 therefore holds only for a convex set, which we must not simply assume.

29.3.4 Tests of convexity (preizkusi konveksnosti)

Definition 29.17 requires inequality (29.12) for every pair of points and every \(t\). This is rarely checked directly. For a function with a continuous gradient the same is told by a different property, which uses the tangent instead of the chord. Figure 29.11 on the right shows it on our function \(V\), drawn over the same axes as on the left: the orange tangent at the point \(h_0 = 3\) m, that is, the line with slope \(V'(h_0)\) that touches the graph at this point, lies below the graph. We compute in the units \(F a/\sigma_0\): \(V/(F a/\sigma_0) = 3{,}4167\), \(V' = -0{,}6389\) per metre. At \(h = 1{,}5\) the tangent is at \(3{,}4167 - 0{,}6389 \cdot (1{,}5 - 3) = 4{,}3750\) and the graph at \(5{,}7083\), at \(h = 8\) the tangent is at \(0{,}2222\) and the graph at \(3{,}0000\). The tangent at the point \(h = 8\) m, of slope \(0{,}125\) per metre, also lies below the graph. This is no accident. Since the chord and the graph meet at the endpoint, the slope of the chord cannot be smaller than the slope of the tangent, and the test follows from this.

Lemma 29.20 Convexity and the tangent plane (konveksnost in tangentna ravnina)

Let \(U\) be an open convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(f\) a continuously differentiable function on \(U\) (definition 8.22, item 4).

  1. The function \(f\) is convex on \(U\) if and only if for every two points \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\)
    \[f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x) + \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x) . \tag{29.14}\]
  2. If the strict inequality holds in (29.14) for every pair \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), then \(f\) is strictly convex.
Proof

We must show both directions of the first part. The direction from convexity to (29.14) follows from the chord lying above the graph with the same start, and the graph must lie below it also in the limit. Conversely we add two tangent inequalities.

  1. Let \(f\) be convex and \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\), \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), \(\vek d = \vek y - \vek x\). We define \(g(t) = f(\vek x + t\,\vek d)\). By lemma 8.28, \(g\) is differentiable at \(t = 0\) and \(g'(0) = \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot\vek d\).
  2. For \(0 < t \le 1\), by (29.12), \(g(t) = f\big((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\big) \le (1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) = g(0) + t\,\big(f(\vek y) - f(\vek x)\big)\). Hence \(\big(g(t) - g(0)\big)/t \le f(\vek y) - f(\vek x)\).
  3. As \(t \to 0\) from the right, the left side has the limit \(g'(0)\), and the inequality is kept in the limit. So \(\nabla f(\vek x)\cdot\vek d \le f(\vek y) - f(\vek x)\), that is, (29.14).
  4. Conversely, let (29.14) hold for all pairs. For \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\) and \(0 < t < 1\) let \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\), which is in \(U\). Inequality (29.14) at the point \(\vek z\) for \(\vek x\) and for \(\vek y\) gives \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek z) + \nabla f(\vek z)\cdot(\vek x - \vek z)\) and \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek z) + \nabla f(\vek z)\cdot(\vek y - \vek z)\).
  5. We multiply the first by \(1 - t > 0\), the second by \(t > 0\) and add: \((1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek z) + \nabla f(\vek z)\cdot\big((1 - t)(\vek x - \vek z) + t\,(\vek y - \vek z)\big)\). The vector in the bracket is \((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y - \vek z = \vek 0\), so \((1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek z)\), that is, (29.12).
  6. Second part: if the inequality in step 4 is strict, which holds for \(\vek x \ne \vek z\) and \(\vek y \ne \vek z\), that is, for \(0 < t < 1\) and \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), the sum in step 5 is strict too.

Source: CHK §3.2 (PDF p. 47-48) states only the condition with a monotone gradient (theorem 3.1), without proof. The proof is not from the source.

The meaning of the right side of (29.14) is this: the function \(\vek y \mapsto f(\vek x) + \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x)\) is a plane (for one coordinate a line) that touches the graph at \(\vek x\) with the same gradient, and we call it the tangent plane (tangentna ravnina). The inequality says: a convex function lies above each of its tangent planes. The consequence for finding a minimum is immediate.

Corollary 29.21 Stationary point of a convex function (stacionarna točka konveksne funkcije)

Let \(U\) be an open convex set and \(f\) a continuously differentiable convex function on \(U\).

  1. If \(\nabla f(\vek x^*) = \vek 0\), then \(\vek x^*\) is a global minimum of \(f\) on \(U\).
  2. Let \(S \subset U\) be a convex set and \(\vek x^* \in S\). If \(\nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x^*) \ge 0\) for every \(\vek y \in S\), then \(\vek x^*\) is a global minimum of \(f\) on \(S\).
Proof

We must show that both parts are a consequence of inequality (29.14).

  1. By lemma 29.20, for every \(\vek y \in S\) we have \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x^*) + \nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x^*)\).
  2. In the second part the scalar product in this inequality is nonnegative, so \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x^*)\). The first part is a special case with \(S = U\), where the product is zero.

Source: For functionals: theorem 5.73 (CHK §3.2, PDF p. 46-48). The proof is not from the source.

The corollary says that for a convex function we have no peaks and saddles: every stationary point is a bottom. We need the second part of the corollary in the next section, when the feasible set is not the whole space. One more condition, which we check with derivatives and not with an inequality for every pair of points.

Lemma 29.22 Convexity by the Hessian matrix (konveksnost po Hessejevi matriki)

Let \(U\) be an open convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(f\) a twice continuously differentiable function on \(U\) with the Hessian matrix \(\mat K(\vek x)\) (definition 8.61).

  1. If \(\mat K(\vek x)\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15) at every point \(\vek x \in U\), then \(f\) is convex on \(U\).
  2. If \(\mat K(\vek x)\) is positive definite (definition 6.27) at every point \(\vek x \in U\), then \(f\) is strictly convex on \(U\).
Proof

We must show the tangent inequality (29.14). We treat the values of \(f\) on the segment from \(\vek x\) to \(\vek y\) as a function of one variable and use theorem 8.60, and the second derivative of this function is the quadratic form of the Hessian matrix.

  1. Let \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\), \(\vek x \ne \vek y\) and \(\vek d = \vek y - \vek x\). We define \(g(s) = f(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\) for \(s \in [0, 1]\). The points \(\vek x + s\,\vek d\) are in \(U\), because \(U\) is convex.
  2. By lemma 8.28, applied to \(f\) and to every partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), which is continuously differentiable, \(g'(s) = \nabla f(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\cdot\vek d\) is continuous and \(g''(s) = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{i}}\,K_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek d^\T\mat K(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\,\vek d\) (as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 8.63).
  3. By theorem 8.60 with \(x_0 = 0\) and \(x = 1\) there is \(c \in (0, 1)\) with \(g(1) = g(0) + g'(0) + \tfrac12 g''(c)\), that is, \(f(\vek y) = f(\vek x) + \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot\vek d + \tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K(\vek x + c\,\vek d)\,\vek d\).
  4. In the first part the last term is \(\ge 0\) by the definition of positive semidefiniteness, so (29.14) holds and by lemma 29.20 \(f\) is convex.
  5. In the second part the last term is \(> 0\), because \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\). Inequality (29.14) is strict for every pair \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), and by the second part of lemma 29.20 \(f\) is strictly convex.

Source: CHK theorem 3.2 (PDF p. 48) (with the converse: a convex function has a positive semidefinite matrix), without proof. The proof is not from the source.

The lemma states only one direction. For a convex function the second derivative at a point cannot be negative, which CHK says (theorem 3.2, PDF p. 48), we do not prove this direction because we do not need it.

Example 29.23 The volume of the truss is convex in the height (prostornina paličja kot funkcija višine je konveksna)

Take \(V(h) = F\,(2a^2 + h^2)/(h\,\sigma_0)\) on the open convex set \(U = \{h > 0\}\) (an interval). The Hessian matrix of one variable is \(1 \times 1\) and equals \(V''(h)\), and positive semidefiniteness means \(d\,V''\,d \ge 0\) for every \(d\). We differentiate: \(V(h) = (F/\sigma_0)\,(2a^2/h + h)\), \(V'(h) = (F/\sigma_0)\,(1 - 2a^2/h^2)\) and \(V''(h) = 4F a^2/(h^3\,\sigma_0)\). This is positive at every \(h > 0\), so \(\mat K\) is positive definite and \(V\) is strictly convex on \(U\) by lemma 29.22. With the unit \(F a/\sigma_0 = 181{,}82\) cm\(^3\) we have \(V''/(F a/\sigma_0) = 4a/h^3 = 16/h^3\) per m\(^2\): \(4{,}7407\) at \(1{,}5\) m, \(0{,}5926\) at \(3\) m, \(0{,}0884\) at \(a\sqrt2 = 5{,}6569\) m and \(0{,}0312\) at \(8\) m (NumPy, num-03.py). The derivative is zero at \(h = a\sqrt2\), so by corollary 29.21 this is the global minimum on \(U\), not only a minimum nearby: \(V = 514{,}3\) cm\(^3\), the volume at \(h = 3\) m (\(621{,}2\) cm\(^3\)) and at \(h = 8\) m (\(545{,}5\) cm\(^3\)) is larger, as figure 29.11 shows. The small value of \(V''\) at large \(h\) says that the graph is almost flat there, and we cannot determine the minimum precisely: at \(h = 8\) m the volume is only \(6\) % above the least one (\(3{,}0000/2{,}8284 = 1{,}060\)).

Figure 29.9 is an example where the lemma does not hold. For the function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + 0{,}4\,x\) we have \(f''(x) = 12x^2 - 4\), and at the peak \(x_2 = 0{,}1010\) \(f'' = -3{,}88 < 0\), so the matrix \([f'']\) is not positive semidefinite and the function is not convex. The tangent at \(x_2\) is horizontal at \(1{,}0201\), and the graph goes below it at \(x_1\), down to \(-0{,}4095\). This is exactly the reverse of the tangent inequality (29.14). The lemma is a sufficient condition: for \(f(x) = x^4\) we have \(f''(0) = 0\), yet the function is strictly convex (CHK, example 3.2, PDF p. 48), so the positive definiteness of the second part of the lemma is not necessary.

A convex function together with a convex feasible set is called a convex problem. The feasible set arises from constraints \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0\) (the letter \(g\) here is a constraint function, not the gravitational acceleration of section 2.2), and for it the following holds.

Lemma 29.24 The feasible set of convex constraints is convex (dopustna množica konveksnih omejitev je konveksna)

Let \(X\) be a convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(g_1, \dots, g_{\mathrm{m}}\) convex functions on \(X\). Then the set \(S = \{\vek x \in X : g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0,\ i = 1, \dots, m\}\) is convex.

Proof

We must show that for two admissible points every point of the segment between them stays admissible.

  1. Let \(\vek x, \vek y \in S\), \(0 \le t \le 1\) and \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\). The point \(\vek z\) is in \(X\), because \(X\) is convex.
