  3. For the second part: by lemma 29.35, \(\alpha\vek A^*\) has compliance \(C^*/\alpha = C_{\max}\). A design \(\vek B\) with \(C(\vek B) \le C_{\max}\) has the design \(\vek B/\alpha\) with compliance \(C(\vek B/\alpha) = \alpha\,C(\vek B) \le C^*\), so volume \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}} B_{\mathrm{e}}/\alpha \ge V_0\) by the first part, and \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}} B_{\mathrm{e}} \ge \alpha V_0\), which is the volume of the design \(\alpha\vek A^*\).

Source: CHK §5.2.3 (PDF p. 95-97) proves the equivalence of both tasks with equations for the KKT points, labelled (5.25) and (5.26). Our proof from scaling is shorter.

Let us look at this with our numbers. At \(\theta = 30^\circ\) the optimum at \(300\ \text{cm}^3\) has the stress \(45{,}53\) MPa. If we allow the stress \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa (without a safety factor, which is our simplification, because a factor only multiplies every cross-section), we must multiply the cross-sections by \(45{,}53/220\). We get \(A_1 = 32{,}14\ \text{mm}^2\), \(A_2 = 16{,}64\ \text{mm}^2\) and the volume \(62{,}09\ \text{cm}^3\), and the compliance grows by the factor \(220/45{,}53 = 4{,}83\). The truss of bars \(1\) and \(2\) is statically determinate, so by lemma 29.10 the fully stressed design is the smallest under a stress constraint, and its volume \((L_1N_1 + L_2N_2)/\sigma_0 = 62{,}09\ \text{cm}^3\) is the same. Minimum compliance and sizing by stresses are therefore here the same design. That this holds for every truss with one load, we do not claim here.

What have we shown? The compliance of a truss is twice the strain energy and a convex function of the cross-sections. A design at a given volume is best when all bars with material have the same energy density and bars without material no larger one, and the sufficient part of this holds also when the structure matrix is not positive definite. On three bars the topology came out of this condition: at every load one of the three bars got cross-section zero, and at \(\theta = 0\) two did. With this we have kept the promise from chapters 4 and 7: the principle of minimum potential energy and the assembly of the structure matrix were all we needed. How to find the optimum when we do not guess which bars have material is described by section 29.7 with the correction of the cross-sections \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \leftarrow A_{\mathrm{e}}\sqrt{E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2/\lambda}\), whose fixed point is the condition (29.31). We derived the derivative of the compliance here for this case (equation (29.30)), and general derivatives are treated in section 29.6.

Cited, not proved: that the solutions of the problem with a lower bound \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min} > 0\) approach, as \(A_{\min} \to 0\), the solution with the bound zero (CHK §5.2, PDF p. 92: "It may be proven that as ε → 0"). Our sufficient condition from point 1 of theorem 29.37 does not need this restriction. It does not say, however, whether the optimum is unique.

29.6 Sensitivity (občutljivost): how a function responds to an area

In section 29.5 we obtained the optimal areas from one condition that held for all bars at once. For conditions that such a condition does not cover, for example a limit on the deflection, we cannot guess the areas. The procedure of the next section corrects the areas step by step: at the current design it computes how the objective and each constraint change if the area of one bar is increased a little, and chooses new areas on that basis. So it needs, for the objective and for each constraint, the derivative with respect to each design variable. In this section we first show that these derivatives exist, then compute them in three ways and compare how much computation each needs and when it fails.

The model is the wall truss of the chapters on energy principles and on the finite element method for bars (figure 29.21, left). Bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) are fixed to the wall at points \(A\) and \(B\) and meet in the joint \(C\), on which the load \(F = 10\) kN acts downward. Bar \(AC\) is horizontal and \(4\) m long, bar \(BC\) is oblique and \(5\) m long. The design variables are the cross-section areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), collected in the column \(\vek A = (A_1, A_2)\) with \(A_1 = A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_2 = A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). The design at which we compute is the design of section 7.5.2, \(A_1 = A_2 = 100\) mm², steel with \(E = 196\) GPa. The assumptions are the same as there: small displacements, linearly elastic material, the load \(F\) does not depend on the areas. The last assumption is an idealization: we neglect the self-weight of the bars. At \(100\) mm², a total bar length of \(9\) m and a steel density of \(7800\) kg/m³ the mass of both bars is \(7{,}02\) kg and their weight \(68{,}9\) N, which is \(0{,}69\,\%\) of the force \(F\). If we included it, the right-hand side of the equilibrium equation would depend on the areas. The letter \(C\) has two meanings here: the joint \(C\) and the compliance \(C(\vek A)\) of definition 29.32, which we always write with its argument (in chapter 10, \(\mat C\) is the damping matrix).

We draw the figure along with the text. Bar \(AC\) is horizontal, bar \(BC\) runs obliquely to the joint \(C\), where the load \(F\) pulls downward. Under the load bar \(AC\) is compressed, \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}33\) kN, and bar \(BC\) is stretched, \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}67\) kN. The right half is the same truss with a different load, which we need in the section on the adjoint method: a unit force \(1\) N downward at the joint \(C\) and the forces in the bars under it.

The function that interests us is the deflection of the joint \(C\) downward, \(g = -v_{\mathrm{C}}\), where \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the vertical displacement. At our design it is, by section 7.5.2, \(g = 10{,}714\) mm. The limit on this deflection will be the constraint of our problem in the next section.

The displacements of the free unknowns, the horizontal and vertical displacement \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}})\) of the joint \(C\), are determined by the equilibrium equation of theorem 7.18, in which the structure matrix (theorem 7.13) depends on the areas. By lemma 7.28, written for the free unknowns, bar \(e\) contributes the matrix \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) with

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{E}{L_{\mathrm{e}}}\,\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T , \tag{29.32}\]

where \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the column for which the elongation of the bar is \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek u\) (for our bar, fixed to the wall with one end, \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\) at the joint \(C\), with the unit vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\) of the bar, directed from the wall towards \(C\)). The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) does not depend on the areas, so

\[\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek u = \vek f , \qquad \mat K(\vek A) = A_1\,\mat K_1 + A_2\,\mat K_2 . \tag{29.33}\]

Hence \(\partial\mat K/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\). In the nested form of the problem (definition 29.2) \(\vek u\) is a function of the areas, so every function \(g(\vek A, \vek u)\) of displacements and areas is also a function of the areas alone, \(\hat g(\vek A) = g(\vek A, \vek u(\vek A))\).

Definition 29.40 Sensitivity (občutljivost)

Let \(\vek A = (A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{n}})\) be the column of design variables (definition 29.1), \(\vek u(\vek A)\) the solution of equation (29.33) at \(\vek A\) and \(g(\vek A, \vek u)\) a function whose input is \(n\) areas and \(m\) displacements and whose output is a number, continuously differentiable in all inputs. The sensitivity (občutljivost) of the function \(\hat g(\vek A) = g(\vek A, \vek u(\vek A))\) to the design variable \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) at the design \(\vek A\) is the partial derivative

\[\frac{\partial\hat g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}}(\vek A) = \lim_{\mathrm{h}\to 0}\frac{\hat g(\vek A + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{e}}) - \hat g(\vek A)}{h} , \tag{29.34}\]

where \(\vek e_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the column with a one at place \(e\) and zeros elsewhere, provided that the limit exists. It is a number with the unit of the function \(g\) per m². The sensitivities to all variables form the column \(\nabla\hat g = (\partial\hat g/\partial A_1, \dots, \partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{n}})\).

Source: CHK section 6 (PDF p. 103): calls the derivatives of the objective and constraint functions with respect to the design variables "sensitivities" and the procedure "sensitivity analysis". The notation \(\hat g\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) is ours.

The word says how sensitive the function is to a change of the variable: a large derivative means that a small change of the area changes the function strongly. The word must not be confused with the condition number \(\kappa(\mat K)\) of definition 6.31. That is a property of a matrix and tells how errors of the right-hand side are amplified when the system is solved. The sensitivity of this definition is the derivative of a function with respect to an area. The words that follow them tell them apart: "condition number of a matrix", "sensitivity of a function to an area".

29.6.1 Finite differences

The simplest way is to really change the design and see what happens. We increase the area \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) by a small number \(h > 0\), solve equation (29.33) again, compute \(\hat g\) and divide the difference by \(h\). This is the forward difference quotient (količnik naprej)

\[D_{\mathrm{h}} = \frac{\hat g(\vek A + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{e}}) - \hat g(\vek A)}{h} . \tag{29.35}\]

By definition 29.40 it approximates the sensitivity for small \(h\). How small is told by the next lemma, and we compare its estimate with a computation on our truss in figure 29.22.

Lemma 29.41 Error of the forward difference quotient (napaka količnika naprej)

Let \(\varphi(t) = \hat g(\vek A + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{e}})\) for \(t \in [0, h]\) be a function with continuous derivative \(\varphi'\) on \([0, h]\) and with a derivative \(\varphi''\) on \((0, h)\), and let \(|\varphi''| \le M\) on \((0, h)\). Let each of the computed values \(\varphi(0)\) and \(\varphi(h)\) be wrong by at most \(\delta > 0\) (the round-off error in solving equation (29.33)) and \(M > 0\). Then for the quotient \(\tilde D_{\mathrm{h}}\) of the two computed values, with the subtraction and the division by \(h\) taken as exact,

\[\big|\tilde D_{\mathrm{h}} - \varphi'(0)\big| \le \tfrac12\,M\,h + \frac{2\,\delta}{h} . \tag{29.36}\]

For \(h > 0\) the right-hand side is smallest at \(h_* = 2\sqrt{\delta/M}\) and there it equals \(2\sqrt{\delta\,M}\).

Idea

The error has two sources. The difference \(\varphi(h) - \varphi(0)\) replaces the derivative by a secant, which is the truncation error, growing with \(h\) (by theorem 8.60). But the computed values are inexact, and their difference is divided by \(h\), so the round-off error grows as \(h\) falls.

Proof

We must show estimate (29.36) and its minimum.

  1. By theorem 8.60 for \(f = \varphi\), \(x_0 = 0\), \(x = h\) there is a point \(c \in (0, h)\) with \(\varphi(h) = \varphi(0) + \varphi'(0)\,h + \tfrac12\varphi''(c)\,h^2\). Divide by \(h\): the exact quotient \(D_{\mathrm{h}} = \big(\varphi(h) - \varphi(0)\big)/h\) satisfies \(D_{\mathrm{h}} - \varphi'(0) = \tfrac12\varphi''(c)\,h\), in absolute value at most \(\tfrac12 M h\).
  2. The computed values differ from the exact ones by at most \(\delta\) each, so the computed difference differs from the exact one by at most \(2\delta\) and the quotient by at most \(2\delta/h\), that is \(|\tilde D_{\mathrm{h}} - D_{\mathrm{h}}| \le 2\delta/h\).
  3. The triangle inequality for \(\tilde D_{\mathrm{h}} - \varphi'(0) = (\tilde D_{\mathrm{h}} - D_{\mathrm{h}}) + (D_{\mathrm{h}} - \varphi'(0))\) gives (29.36).
  4. The right-hand side \(r(h) = \tfrac12 M h + 2\delta/h\) has derivative \(r'(h) = \tfrac12 M - 2\delta/h^2\), which is zero at \(h_*^2 = 4\delta/M\), that is \(h_* = 2\sqrt{\delta/M}\). The second derivative \(r''(h) = 4\delta/h^3\) is positive, so this is the minimum, \(r(h_*) = \sqrt{\delta M} + \sqrt{\delta M} = 2\sqrt{\delta M}\).

Source: CHK section 6.1 (PDF pp. 103-104): the truncation error \(O(h)\) and the error from the cancellation of numbers, which for small \(h\) grows "dramatically", equation (6.1). The estimate (29.36) with the sum of both and \(h_*\) is not from the source.

We test the lemma on the truss. The area of bar \(AC\) is the only variable, the rest stays at \(100\) mm². The truss is statically determinate, so the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) are fixed by equilibrium, and by theorem 4.95 the deflection is \(\varphi(t) = c_1/(A_1 + t) + c_2/A_2\) with \(c_{\mathrm{e}} = \hat N_{\mathrm{e}} N_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}/E\), where \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -4/3\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5/3\) are the forces under a unit force downward at the joint \(C\) (section 4.1.4). So \(c_1 = (4/3)(13\,333)(4)/(196 \cdot 10^9) = 3{,}628 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m³ and \(c_2 = 7{,}086 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m³. Hence \(\varphi'(0) = -c_1/A_1^2 = -36{,}281\) m/m² and \(\varphi''(t) = 2c_1/(A_1 + t)^3\), which falls with \(t\), so \(M = \varphi''(0) = 7{,}256 \cdot 10^{5}\) m⁻³. We take the round-off error \(\delta = 1{,}11 \cdot 10^{-16}\,\varphi(0) = 1{,}19 \cdot 10^{-18}\) m. This is a choice that the computation confirms: at all eight steps we tried, the measured error is below the estimate. We measure the step relatively, \(s = h/A_1\), and the error relatively, \(r = |\tilde D_{\mathrm{h}} - \varphi'(0)|/|\varphi'(0)|\). The truncation term is then \(\tfrac12 M h/|\varphi'(0)| = s\), and the round-off term is \(k/s\) with \(k = 2\delta/(A_1|\varphi'(0)|) = 6{,}56 \cdot 10^{-16}\).

\(s\) measured \(r\) estimate \(s + k/s\)
\(10^{-1}\) \(9{,}1 \cdot 10^{-2}\) \(1{,}0 \cdot 10^{-1}\)
\(10^{-4}\) \(1{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(1{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
\(10^{-8}\) \(8{,}6 \cdot 10^{-9}\) \(7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-8}\)
\(10^{-10}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(6{,}6 \cdot 10^{-6}\)
\(10^{-12}\) \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(6{,}6 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
\(10^{-14}\) \(4{,}1 \cdot 10^{-3}\) \(6{,}6 \cdot 10^{-2}\)

Figure 29.22 draws all eight steps. On the horizontal axis is the step \(s\), on the vertical one the error \(r\), both on a logarithmic scale: equal distances on an axis mean equal factors. On such a scale the functions \(r = s\) and \(r = k/s\) are straight lines. At large steps the measured error agrees with the truncation term, which is \(r = s\). At small steps the round-off term takes over, \(r = k/s\), which grows as the step falls. The estimate is their sum, and the measured points lie below it. The smallest estimate is at the step \(s_* = \sqrt{k} = 2{,}6 \cdot 10^{-8}\), that is \(h_* = 2{,}56 \cdot 10^{-12}\) m², and the estimate is there \(2\sqrt{k} = 5{,}1 \cdot 10^{-8}\). At this step the estimate guarantees about seven correct digits of the sensitivity. The measured error at \(s = 10^{-8}\), \(8{,}6 \cdot 10^{-9}\), is somewhat smaller still, because the estimate is only an upper bound.

The lemma says what the step should be, and the test shows what happens at a wrong one. Take first a step that is too small, \(s = 10^{-14}\). The truncation term there is only \(10^{-14}\), and by it alone we would get the derivative almost exactly. But the difference \(\varphi(h) - \varphi(0) = -36{,}28 \cdot 10^{-18}\) m is only \(3{,}4 \cdot 10^{-15}\) of the value of the deflection. In absolute value it is only \(30\) times the round-off error \(\delta = 1{,}19 \cdot 10^{-18}\) m of each of the two values, so the error of the difference can be up to \(2\delta/(36{,}28 \cdot 10^{-18}\ \text{m}) = 6{,}6\,\%\) of the difference. This is the round-off term \(k/s\) of the table. The measured error is \(4{,}1 \cdot 10^{-3}\), which is \(4{,}8 \cdot 10^{5}\) times more than the best measured one at \(s = 10^{-8}\). The truncation term alone does not predict this, because it does not include round-off. A step that is too small is therefore an error that no further reduction of the step removes, it only makes it larger.

At a step that is too large, \(s = 10^{-1}\), the error is of another kind and we see its cause at once: we replaced the derivative by a secant across \(10\,\%\) of the area. For the function \(c/A\) we can even write it exactly: \(\big(c/(A(1+s)) - c/A\big)/h = -c/(A^2(1+s))\), so the relative error is \(1 - 1/(1+s) = s/(1+s) = 0{,}0909\). It is smaller than the estimate \(s\) because \(\varphi''\) falls.

The difference across both sides, \(D_{\mathrm{h}}^{\mathrm{c}} = \big(\hat g(\vek A + h\vek e_{\mathrm{e}}) - \hat g(\vek A - h\vek e_{\mathrm{e}})\big)/(2h)\), has a truncation error of order \(h^2\) (CHK, equation (6.2), PDF p. 104, stated there without proof), and on the same truss at \(s = 10^{-4}\) it is exact to \(1{,}0 \cdot 10^{-8}\) instead of \(1{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\). But it costs two solutions per variable instead of one. A gradient with \(n\) variables needs \(n\) extra solutions of equation (29.33) with the forward difference, \(2n\) with the difference across both sides, besides the solution at the design itself. CHK (PDF p. 104) says of both that they can be very inexact and expensive, but are easy to write down. The two analytic ways are therefore treated by the statements below.

29.6.2 The direct method

Instead of changing the design, we differentiate the equilibrium equation. If both sides are equal for every \(\vek A\), so are their derivatives. For this we must know that \(\vek u\) as a function of the areas has a derivative at all, and that is what the implicit function theorem guarantees.

Lemma 29.42 Direct method (neposredna metoda)

Let \(\mat K(\vek A) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) with given symmetric matrices \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) of order \(m\), the right-hand side \(\vek f(\vek A)\) continuously differentiable and \(\vek A^*\) a design at which \(\mat K(\vek A^*)\) is positive definite. Then in a neighbourhood of \(\vek A^*\) the solution \(\vek u(\vek A)\) of the equation \(\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek u = \vek f(\vek A)\) is a continuously differentiable function of the areas, and its derivative \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} = \partial\vek u/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\) at \(\vek A^*\) solves a system with the same matrix,

\[\mat K\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek p_{\mathrm{e}} , \qquad \vek p_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{\partial\vek f}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek u . \tag{29.37}\]

For the function \(g(\vek A, \vek u)\) of definition 29.40 it follows that \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} + (\partial g/\partial\vek u)\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\partial g/\partial\vek u\) is the row with entries \(\partial g/\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Idea

Solving \(\vek F(\vek A, \vek u) = \mat K(\vek A)\,\vek u - \vek f(\vek A) = \vek 0\) for the unknowns \(\vek u\) at given \(\vek A\) is exactly a case of the implicit function theorem, whose pivot condition is ensured by positive definiteness.

Proof

We must show that theorem 8.34 applies to \(\vek F\), and that its derivative (8.19) gives (29.37).

  1. The points \((\vek A, \vek u)\) have \(n + m\) coordinates. The term \(\mat K(\vek A)\vek u\) is a polynomial in \(\vek A\) and \(\vek u\), \(\vek f\) is continuously differentiable, so \(\vek F\) is continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\). The point \((\vek A^*, \vek u^*)\) with \(\vek u^* = \mat K(\vek A^*)^{-1}\vek f(\vek A^*)\) satisfies \(\vek F = \vek 0\).
  2. The matrix \(\partial\vek F/\partial\vek u = \mat K(\vek A)\) has, by theorem 6.29, all \(m\) pivots (definition 8.20) at \(\vek A^*\), because it is positive definite. The condition of theorem 8.34 is met.
  3. The theorem gives a continuously differentiable \(\vek u(\vek A)\) near \(\vek A^*\) with \(\vek F(\vek A, \vek u(\vek A)) = \vek 0\), and by equation (8.19), \(\partial\vek u/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -\mat K^{-1}\,\partial\vek F/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  4. Column \(e\) of the matrix \(\partial\vek F/\partial\vek A\) is \(\partial\vek F/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek u - \partial\vek f/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -\vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\), because \(\partial\mat K/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\). Hence \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat K^{-1}\vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\), which is (29.37).
  5. The function \(\hat g(\vek A) = g(\vek A, \vek u(\vek A))\) is composed of continuously differentiable maps. By the chain rule (lemma 8.29), \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}} (\partial g/\partial u_{\mathrm{r}})\,\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\), which is the last claim.

Source: CHK section 6.2.1 (PDF pp. 104-105), equation (6.4) and the chain rule (6.3). CHK obtains equation (29.37) by differentiating the equilibrium equation. The proof that the derivative exists, by the implicit function theorem, is not from the source.

The right-hand side \(\vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\) has the form of a load on the joints, so CHK calls it a pseudo-load (navidezna obremenitev): equation (29.37) is the equilibrium equation, only that instead of the force \(\vek F\) the load \(\vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\) acts on the joint \(C\). When the matrix \(\mat K\) is factorized (chapter 7), each such solution takes only a forward and a back substitution (CHK, PDF pp. 104-105), but it must be done for each of the \(n\) areas.

On our truss \(\vek f = (0, -10\,000)\) N, independent of the areas, so \(\vek p_{\mathrm{e}} = -\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek u\) with \(\vek u = (-2{,}7211, -10{,}7143)\) mm. Two solutions of equation (29.37) give

\[\vek w_{\mathrm{AC}} = (0{,}027211,\ 0{,}036281)\ \text{mm/mm}^2 , \qquad \vek w_{\mathrm{BC}} = (0,\ 0{,}070862)\ \text{mm/mm}^2 .\]

When the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) is increased a little by \(\Delta A\), the joint \(C\) moves about \(0{,}027\,\Delta A\) mm/mm² to the right and \(0{,}036\,\Delta A\) mm/mm² upward, and the deflection decreases: \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}036281\) mm/mm² \(= -36{,}281\) m/m². The sensitivity to \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) is \(-70{,}862\) m/m². The zero in \(\vek w_{\mathrm{BC}}\) is no accident: by the unit force method (theorem 4.95, \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\), \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\)) the horizontal displacement of the joint \(C\) equals the elongation of bar \(AC\), which does not depend on \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\).

29.6.3 The adjoint method

The direct method solves one system per variable, even when we want the sensitivity of a single function. We turn the question around: instead of "how does \(\vek u\) change with \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\)" we ask "how does one function \(g\) respond to each displacement". The answer is one solution for all \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Theorem 29.43 Adjoint method (prirejena metoda)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\vek f\) and \(\vek A^*\) be as in lemma 29.42 (so \(\mat K\) is positive definite at \(\vek A^*\)) and \(g(\vek A, \vek u)\) as in definition 29.40. Let \(\vek\lambda\) be the solution of the adjoint system (prirejeni sistem)

\[\mat K\,\vek\lambda = \Big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\vek u}\Big)^\T . \tag{29.38}\]

Then at \(\vek A^*\), for every \(e\),

\[\frac{\partial\hat g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}} + \vek\lambda^\T\Big(\frac{\partial\vek f}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek u\Big) , \tag{29.39}\]

and for all \(n\) areas only one system (29.38) is needed for each function \(g\).

Idea

The derivative \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\) of lemma 29.42 enters the sensitivity only through the row \(\partial g/\partial\vek u\). If this row already contains \(\mat K\), which multiplies \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\) into \(\vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\), we arrive at \(\vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\) without \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Proof

We must show that the row \(\partial g/\partial\vek u\) can be written as \(\vek\lambda^\T\mat K\), which eliminates \(\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\).

  1. The matrix \(\mat K\) is positive definite, so by theorem 6.29 system (29.38) has exactly one solution \(\vek\lambda\) for every right-hand side.
  2. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric (corollary 7.14), so transposing equation (29.38) gives \(\partial g/\partial\vek u = \vek\lambda^\T\mat K\).
  3. By lemma 29.42, \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} + (\partial g/\partial\vek u)\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} = \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} + \vek\lambda^\T\,\mat K\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  4. By equation (29.37), \(\mat K\,\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek p_{\mathrm{e}} = \partial\vek f/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u\). Substituting gives (29.39).
  5. The vector \(\vek\lambda\) does not depend on \(e\), so one system (29.38) serves all variables.

Source: CHK section 6.2.2 (PDF pp. 105-106), equations (6.7) and (6.8), where the proof is by substituting (6.4) into (6.6). The comparison of costs (PDF p. 106) we summarize below. The notation with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) is ours.

The name comes from the matrix of system (29.38) being the adjoint (transposed) matrix of the system of the direct method. For symmetric \(\mat K\) they are the same, as for every truss of ours, but in general it would be the transpose. Let us compare costs. The direct method solves \(n\) systems \(\mat K\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek p_{\mathrm{e}}\), one for each area. The adjoint method solves one for each function that we differentiate, that is for the objective and each of the \(l\) constraints, in all \(l + 1\). For a truss with \(n = 100\) bars and one deflection constraint this is \(100\) against \(2\) solutions with a factorized matrix. CHK (PDF p. 106) summarizes: the adjoint method is better when there are fewer constraints than design variables, otherwise the direct one. On our truss the objective is the volume \(V = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\partial V/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = L_{\mathrm{e}}\) and no system, so the adjoint method needs one system for the deflection, the direct method two, and at \(n = 2\) the advantage is not yet large.

The theorem holds when the matrix \(\mat K\) is positive definite, and for a truss we lose it when the area of a bar drops to zero. Let us test it: we reduce the area of bar \(BC\) and \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 100\) mm² stays. Bar \(AC\) is horizontal and cannot carry a vertical force, so the joint \(C\) moves more and more. The deflection and the sensitivity to \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), computed by theorem 29.43 and from the closed form \(-c_2/A_{\mathrm{BC}}^2\) (both give the same), are:

\(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) in mm² deflection \(g\) in mm \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) in mm/mm²
\(100\) \(10{,}7\) \(-0{,}0709\)
\(10\) \(74{,}5\) \(-7{,}09\)
\(1\) \(712\) \(-709\)
\(0{,}1\) \(7090\) \(-70\,862\)

Each row has a \(10\) times smaller area and a \(100\) times larger sensitivity, as for \(1/A^2\). At \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), \(\mat K = A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{AC}}\) has a zero second row and column, it is singular (determinant zero), the adjoint system (29.38) has no solution and the theorem does not apply. The lower two rows have deflections of \(0{,}71\) m and \(7{,}1\) m on a truss with a span of \(4\) m, where the small-displacement model of section 7.5.2 no longer holds. The formula therefore says only that the sensitivity grows beyond all bounds as the bar vanishes, not what the deflection of such a bar would really be. Section 29.5 has the same difficulty for bars whose area falls toward zero.

29.6.4 Sensitivity of the compliance

For the compliance \(C(\vek A) = \vek f^\T\vek u\) (definition 29.32) the function \(g = \vek f^\T\vek u\) is itself part of the equilibrium equation, and the theorem will give a special, simple result.

Corollary 29.44 Sensitivity of the compliance (občutljivost podajnosti)

Let \(\vek f\) be independent of the areas and \(\mat K(\vek A) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) positive definite at \(\vek A\), with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) from equation (29.32). Let bar \(e\) have the elongation \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} = \Delta L_{\mathrm{e}}/L_{\mathrm{e}}\). Then

\[\frac{\partial C}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}} = -\,\vek u^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek u = -E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{e}} = -\frac{2\,U_{\mathrm{e}}}{A_{\mathrm{e}}} , \tag{29.40}\]

where \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\,A_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the strain energy of bar \(e\). The sensitivity is negative for every bar: more material in any bar decreases the compliance.

Idea

For \(g = \vek f^\T\vek u\) the adjoint system is the equilibrium equation, so the adjoint solution is \(\vek u\) itself and we need no new system.

Proof

We must show that theorem 29.43 gives \(\vek\lambda = \vek u\), and then express \(\vek u^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u\) by the elongation.

  1. For \(g(\vek A, \vek u) = \vek f^\T\vek u\), \(\partial g/\partial\vek A = \vek 0\) and \(\partial g/\partial\vek u = \vek f^\T\). The adjoint system (29.38) is \(\mat K\vek\lambda = \vek f\), which is the equilibrium equation, so \(\vek\lambda = \vek u\).
  2. Since \(\partial\vek f/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\), equation (29.39) gives \(\partial C/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -\vek u^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u\).
  3. By equation (29.32), \(\vek u^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u = (E/L_{\mathrm{e}})\,(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek u)^2 = (E/L_{\mathrm{e}})\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{e}}^2\), because \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek u\) is the elongation of the bar. With \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{e}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}\) this is \(E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  4. By definition 4.2 with \(w = \tfrac12 E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) constant along the bar, \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2A_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}\), so \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2L_{\mathrm{e}} = 2U_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Source: CHK examples 6.1 and 6.2 (PDF pp. 105-106): equation (6.5) at \(\partial\vek f/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) and the conclusion \(\vek\lambda = \vek u\). The expression with the elongation and with the energy of the bar is not from the source.

By theorem 29.37, at minimum compliance \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) is the same in all bars with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). By equation (29.40) this is \(-\partial C/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\) divided by \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\): every bar with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) gives, at the optimum, the same decrease of compliance per unit volume, \(-\partial C/\partial(A_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}) = E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\).

Example 29.45 Sensitivities of the wall truss (občutljivosti stenskega paličja)

The wall truss of the introduction of this section has, by section 7.5.2, the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}33\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}67\) kN and the compliance \(C = 107{,}14\) J. Let \(g = -v_{\mathrm{C}}\) be the deflection. The adjoint system (29.38) is \(\mat K\vek\lambda = (0, -1)^\T\), which is the equilibrium system with a unit force \(1\) N downward at the joint \(C\): the solution is \(\vek\lambda = \vek u/(10\,000\ \text{N}) = (-2{,}7211, -10{,}7143)\cdot 10^{-7}\) m/N. The adjoint load is thus the unit force of the unit force method (theorem 4.95, \(\vek d = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\)), and the axial forces are, by the right half of the figure, \(\hat N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -4/3\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5/3\), per unit force.

  1. The displacements \(\vek\lambda\) are the displacements under the unit force, for which bar \(e\) carries the force \(\hat N_{\mathrm{e}}\). The elongation of a bar is its force times \(L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}})\), so \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek\lambda = \hat N_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}})\) and \(\vek b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\vek u = N_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}})\). By equation (29.32), \(\vek\lambda^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u = (E/L_{\mathrm{e}})\,(\hat N_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}}))\,(N_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}})) = \hat N_{\mathrm{e}}\,N_{\mathrm{e}}\,L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}}^2)\) and by equation (29.39) \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -\hat N_{\mathrm{e}}\,N_{\mathrm{e}}\,L_{\mathrm{e}}/(E\,A_{\mathrm{e}}^2)\).
  2. Bar \(AC\): \(-(-4/3)(-13\,333)(4)/(196\cdot 10^9\cdot (10^{-4})^2) = -36{,}281\) m/m². Bar \(BC\): \(-(5/3)(16\,667)(5)/(196\cdot 10^9\cdot(10^{-4})^2) = -70{,}862\) m/m². The same numbers were given by the direct method and the adjoint equation (29.39), and a third time by the closed form: for a truss whose forces are fixed by equilibrium, \(g = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \hat N_{\mathrm{e}}N_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}})\), and its derivative with respect to \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the one above.
  3. A check. Multiply all areas by \(s\): the matrix \(\mat K\) is multiplied by \(s\), the solution \(\vek u\) is divided by \(s\), so \(g(s\vek A) = g(\vek A)/s\). By the chain rule at \(s = 1\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -g\): \(100\cdot(-0{,}036281) + 100\cdot(-0{,}070862) = -10{,}714\) mm, which is \(-g\).
  4. Compliance: \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{AC}}^2 = 196 \cdot 10^9 \cdot (-6{,}803 \cdot 10^{-4})^2 = 90{,}70\) kJ/m³ and \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{BC}}^2 = 196\cdot 10^9\cdot(8{,}503\cdot 10^{-4})^2 = 141{,}72\) kJ/m³. By equation (29.40), \(\partial C/\partial A_{\mathrm{AC}} = -362\,812\) J/m² \(= -0{,}3628\) J/mm² and \(\partial C/\partial A_{\mathrm{BC}} = -0{,}7086\) J/mm², which is \(F\,\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\) (\(F = 10\) kN). The check with \(s\): \(100\cdot(-0{,}3628 - 0{,}7086) = -107{,}14\) J \(= -C\).

For this truss the expression \(\hat N_{\mathrm{e}} N_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}}^2)\) is computed without solving anything, because \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{e}}\) are fixed by equilibrium. For a statically indeterminate truss the forces depend on the areas. The deflection there is no longer a sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) with constant \(c_{\mathrm{e}}\), and we do not get the forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\hat N_{\mathrm{e}}\) without solving the systems for \(\vek u\) and \(\vek\lambda\). The adjoint equation (29.39) holds there too, since it uses only the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the solutions \(\vek u\) and \(\vek\lambda\). Step 1 of the example uses only the elongations of the bar under these two solutions, so \(\partial\hat g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -\hat N_{\mathrm{e}}N_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}/(EA_{\mathrm{e}}^2)\) holds there as well, with the two forces computed from \(\vek u\) and \(\vek\lambda\).

We now have the derivative of the deflection and of the compliance with respect to each area, and we compute it without repeating the whole computation for each area separately. The next section uses these derivatives to correct the design step by step.

29.7 Sequential approximations (zaporedne aproksimacije)

We optimized the wall truss in section 29.2 by hand, because the forces in the bars are known from equilibrium before we know the areas. The displacement of joint \(C\) was a formula in the areas, and the least volume at a bounded displacement came from a calculation on paper. For a truss with a hundred bars and several load cases there is no such formula. Every value of the objective and of every constraint appears only after we solve the equilibrium \(\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek u = \vek F\), as chapter 7 taught us, and again for every new design. How do we attack the problem when solving the equilibrium costs more than everything else? Sequential approximations answer as follows: whatever we cannot compute quickly, we replace at each step by a function we can, solve the replaced problem, and repeat the step. This section explains three such replacements, sequential linear programming, convex linearization and the optimality criteria update, and tests each on trusses we already know.

29.7.1 A loop with an explicit subproblem (zanka z eksplicitno podnalogo)

The idea of accepting every design at once is risky, so we begin with the order of work. The problem has the form of definition 29.2: the objective \(f(\vek A)\) and the constraints \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek A) \le 0\) are functions of the design variables \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{n}}\) (the bar areas) alone, and the state \(\vek u\) is eliminated by the equilibrium equation. Figure 29.23 shows the loop described by CHK in section 4.1 (PDF pp. 65-66).

We begin with the design \(\vek A^k\), where the index \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) counts the rounds of the loop. For it we solve the equilibrium, as for the truss of chapter 7 (theorem 7.18). Once we know the displacements, we compute the values and derivatives of the functions \(f\) and \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) at \(\vek A^k\), the derivatives by the methods of section 29.6. From these numbers we build the approximation, that is, a function written as a formula in \(\vek A\), which we therefore evaluate without solving the equilibrium. We solve the problem with it, which gives the new design \(\vek A^{k+1}\), and the arrow back closes the loop. We stop the loop when the design hardly changes between two rounds.

Definition 29.46 Explicit approximation and subproblem (eksplicitni približek in podnaloga)

Let the problem \(\min f(\vek A)\) subject to \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek A) \le 0\) for \(i = 1, \dots, l\) be given in nested form (definition 29.2), with continuously differentiable \(f\) and \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) on the set of designs with all areas \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). Let \(\vek A^k\) be a design from this set. An explicit approximation of the function \(g\) at \(\vek A^k\) is a function \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) that we compute from the numbers \(g(\vek A^k)\) and \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(\vek A^k)\) by a formula in the areas, without solving the equilibrium. The subproblem at \(\vek A^k\) is the problem

\[\min\ \tilde f^{\,k}(\vek A) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \tilde g_{\mathrm{i}}^{\,k}(\vek A) \le 0 , \quad i = 1, \dots, l , \tag{29.41}\]

and its solution is \(\vek A^{k+1}\).

Source: The loop and the terms are after CHK section 4.1 (PDF pp. 65-66, steps 1 to 6), there with the symbol \(x\) for the design variables. The wording of the definition is ours.

The word "sequential" says that we solve a sequence of subproblems \(k = 0, 1, \dots\), and "explicit" says that each subproblem is written with formulas in \(\vek A\). There are several approximations, and they differ in which function they take. The first is the simplest.

29.7.2 Sequential linear programming (zaporedno linearno programiranje)

The simplest approximation is the tangent plane, that is, linearization. When both sides of the subproblem are linear in \(\vek A\), we call the problem a linear program: the objective is linear and all constraints are linear inequalities. Any ordinary program solves such a problem quickly and reliably, and its solution lies at a vertex of the feasible polygon (as will be seen in figure 29.24).

Definition 29.47 Sequential linear programming, SLP (zaporedno linearno programiranje)

In the setting of definition 29.46 the tangent-plane approximations are

\[\tilde f^{\,k}(\vek A) = f(\vek A^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{n} \frac{\partial f}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}}(\vek A^k)\,(A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^k) , \tag{29.42}\]

and likewise for \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\). The SLP subproblem is a linear program with two additional bounds for each area,

\[\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} \le A_{\mathrm{e}} \le \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} , \qquad e = 1, \dots, n . \tag{29.43}\]

The bounds \(\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k}\) and \(\overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k}\) are the move limit: they ensure that in one round the design does not move too far from the point \(\vek A^k\) where the linearization holds. Without a move limit the bounds are simply the smallest and the largest admissible area \(A_{\min}\) and \(A_{\max}\). With a relative move limit \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) we have \(\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} = \max\{A_{\min},\ (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})\,A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\}\) and \(\overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} = \min\{A_{\max},\ (1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})\,A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\}\).

Source: CHK section 4.2 (PDF pp. 66-67): linearization at \(\vek x^k\), the limits \(l_{\mathrm{j}}^k\) and \(u_{\mathrm{j}}^k\), which are "updated according to some user-defined rule", and the statement that the subproblem is a linear program. The relative form of the limit and the symbol \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) are ours. SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2) writes the same notion with \(m\), which in the chapters on dynamics is a mass.

The name says what we do: a sequence of linear programs (programming here is the old word for solving such problems by a plan, not writing computer code). We test it on a truss we know. The wall truss of section 4.1.4 has the joints \(A = (-4, 0)\) m and \(B = (-4, 3)\) m, the joint \(C = (0, 0)\) with the load \(F = 10\) kN downward, the bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) of lengths \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m and \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m, and \(E = 196\) GPa. The problem: the least volume \(V = L_{\mathrm{AC}}A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) at a downward displacement of joint \(C\) with \(v_{\mathrm{C}} \le \delta = 2\) mm. The idealizations of straight bars, small displacements and a linearly elastic material from chapter 7 hold, and we neglect the weight of the bars. The areas lie between \(1\) mm² and \(10\,000\) mm².

The displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) is a formula in the areas, because the truss is statically determinate: the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}33\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}67\) kN are fixed by equilibrium and do not depend on the areas, and the unit forces are \(n_{\mathrm{AC}} = N_{\mathrm{AC}}/F = -4/3\) and \(n_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5/3\). By the unit force method (theorem 4.95, equation (4.64))

\[v_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \hat N_{\mathrm{e}}\,\frac{N_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}}{E A_{\mathrm{e}}} = \frac{c_{\mathrm{AC}}}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \frac{c_{\mathrm{BC}}}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}} , \qquad c_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{e}}\,n_{\mathrm{e}}\,L_{\mathrm{e}}}{E} , \tag{29.44}\]

with \(c_{\mathrm{AC}} = 3{,}628\cdot 10^{-7}\) m³ and \(c_{\mathrm{BC}} = 7{,}086\cdot 10^{-7}\) m³. At the areas \(100\) mm² of chapter 7 the formula gives \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 10{,}714\) mm, as we computed there. The derivative is \(\partial v_{\mathrm{C}}/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\), at \(100\) mm² this is \(-36{,}28\) and \(-70{,}86\) m per m², as the unit force gives in section 29.6.

We start at \(\vek A^0 = (600, 600)\) mm², where \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 1{,}786\) mm (a feasible design) and \(V = 5400\) cm³. The derivatives there are \(-1{,}008\cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(-1{,}968\cdot 10^{-3}\) mm per mm². The first SLP subproblem is the linear program: the least \(V\) subject to \(v_{\mathrm{C}}(\vek A^0) + \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \partial v_{\mathrm{C}}/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^0) \le \delta\). Figure 29.24 shows the two areas as coordinates.

Look first at the left half of the figure. The axes are logarithmic, because without a move limit the SLP designs are scattered over three orders of magnitude. The blue curve is the set of designs with \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 2\) mm, from formula (29.44): the areas are tied by \(c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}} = \delta\). The grey dashed line is the linearized constraint from \(\vek A^0\). Point 0 is the starting design. The linear program lies at a vertex, and since the linearization of the constraint knows no curvature, only the ratio of cost to benefit decides: bar \(e\) reduces the displacement by \(c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) per unit of area and costs \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\) per unit of area, so it is worth increasing the one with the smaller quotient \(L_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}^2/c_{\mathrm{e}}\). At \(\vek A^0\) this quotient is \(3{,}969\) m² for \(AC\) and \(2{,}540\) m² for \(BC\), so the program gives all the area to \(BC\) and lowers \(AC\) to its lower bound: point 1 is \((1{,}0;\ 797{,}8)\) mm². The linearized constraint there does give \(2{,}000\) mm, but the true displacement is \(363{,}7\) mm: bar \(AC\) with area \(1\) mm² is like a thread.

Lemma 29.48 The linearized SLP constraint admits too much (linearizirana omejitev SLP dopušča preveč)

Let \(g\) be a convex and continuously differentiable function on an open convex set of designs (definition 29.17) and \(\vek A^k\) a design from it. Then every design that satisfies \(g(\vek A) \le 0\) is also feasible for the linearized constraint \(g(\vek A^k) + \nabla g(\vek A^k)\cdot(\vek A - \vek A^k) \le 0\). Therefore, for a linear objective, the value of the SLP subproblem, measured on the same move limits, is at most the least value of the true problem.

Proof

We must show that the feasible set of the true problem is a subset of the feasible set of the subproblem. The key is the tangent plane of a convex function from section 29.3.

  1. By lemma 29.20 on the tangent plane, for convex \(g\) every \(\vek A\) in the set satisfies \(g(\vek A) \ge g(\vek A^k) + \nabla g(\vek A^k)\cdot(\vek A - \vek A^k)\).
  2. If \(g(\vek A) \le 0\), then by step 1 the right-hand side is at most \(g(\vek A) \le 0\), so the linearized constraint holds.
  3. The move limits are the same in both problems. The least value of a linear function \(f\) on a larger set is not larger than on a smaller one, and this is the second claim.

Source: The proof is ours, from lemma 29.20.

The lemma says in which direction the linearization deceives: a convex constraint is softened by linearization, so the program is too easy and pushes the design where the true constraint does not hold. The converse is not guaranteed, and point 1 in the figure is an example. Its values agree with the lemma: the volume \(3993\) cm³ is less than the true least volume \(4764{,}7\) cm³ (a lower bound), and the displacement \(363{,}7\) mm is more than ten times too large. So the lemma does not claim that the subproblem is feasible, and it does not claim that its solution is near the true one.

Example 29.49 Two failures of SLP on the wall truss (dva neuspeha SLP na stenskem paličju)

Without a move limit the designs do not settle. From point 1 the left part of figure 29.24 shows the sequence \((1{,}0;\ 797{,}8)\), \((2{,}0;\ 1{,}0)\), \((1{,}0;\ 2{,}4)\), \((3{,}3;\ 1{,}0)\) mm² and onward \((1{,}0;\ 2{,}3)\), \((3{,}3;\ 1{,}0)\), \((1{,}0;\ 2{,}3)\), \((3{,}3;\ 1{,}0)\). The displacements are \(363{,}7\), \(890{,}1\), \(660{,}4\), \(818{,}9\) mm and then between \(676\) and \(818\) mm, no design is feasible. Each subproblem puts all the material into the bar that looks cheaper at the current areas, and in the next design that bar looks expensive, because its quotient \(L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^2/c_{\mathrm{e}}\) has changed.

With a move limit \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}3\) the designs do not run away, but they do not settle either. The right half of figure 29.24 has linear axes, because the designs now stay between \(300\) and \(700\) mm². The blue curve is again the boundary \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 2\) mm, and the grey dashed line is the linearized constraint from \(\vek A^0\), on which point 1 lies. From \(\vek A^0\) the designs go to \((420{,}0;\ 583{,}3)\), \((546{,}0;\ 496{,}6)\), \((382{,}2;\ 597{,}8)\), \((496{,}9;\ 522{,}1)\), \((347{,}8;\ 640{,}0)\), \((452{,}1;\ 546{,}0)\), \((316{,}5;\ 689{,}5)\), \((411{,}4;\ 575{,}6)\) mm². The displacements are between \(2{,}079\) and \(2{,}174\) mm, always above the limit of \(2\) mm, the volumes between \(4518\) and \(4713\) cm³. The empty circle is the optimum \((464{,}85;\ 581{,}07)\) mm², where the solid grey line \(V = 4764{,}7\) cm³ touches the blue curve. The designs jump back and forth across the optimum, never reach it and never settle there.

Why do they not settle? At the optimum the gradient of the objective must be parallel to the gradient of the constraint, which is the KKT condition of section 29.4: \(L_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu\,c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) for both bars with the same number \(\mu\). At the optimum we indeed have \(L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^2/c_{\mathrm{e}} = 2{,}382\) m² for \(AC\) and \(BC\), and this is \(\mu\). A linear program whose objective is parallel to the constraint has no unique solution: every point on the line is equally good. Near the optimum the objective and the linearized constraint are nearly parallel, so a small difference of the quotients \(L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^2/c_{\mathrm{e}}\) decides which bar is cheaper. The linear program thins the more expensive bar down to the lower move bound or thickens the cheaper one up to the upper bound, and the linearized constraint fixes the area of the other bar. The solution is thus a vertex of the feasible polygon with one area on a move bound and the other on the linearized constraint. In our sequence the area on the bound is always \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\), which alternately shrinks and grows by \(30\) %. After the step the quotients swap, and the next step jumps back: at the points \(1, 3, 5, 7\) bar \(AC\) is the cheaper one, at the points \(2, 4, 6\) bar \(BC\). Since \(0{,}7 \cdot 1{,}3 = 0{,}91\), the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) is \(9\) % smaller after every pair of steps, so the designs in the figure creep up and to the left, and at point 8 bar \(AC\) is still the cheaper one. The displacement stays above \(2\) mm, because by lemma 29.48 the linearized constraint admits too much: the tangent plane of a convex function lies below it.

We do not prove the convergence of loops in this book. The test on this example is enough for the conclusion that SLP is not reliable without a rule for the move limit that shrinks with the rounds (CHK PDF p. 67 says that the choice of the move limits "affects the efficiency considerably").

29.7.3 Convex linearization (konveksna linearizacija)

Why does SLP describe the displacement so badly? Linearization in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) would be exact if the displacement were a linear function of the areas, but by formula (29.44) the displacement is linear in \(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\). Figure 29.25 shows this on one bar: we choose the variable in which the function is closer to a straight line.

The axes show the displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) of the joint as one area varies. The blue curve is \(c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) and is convex and decreasing. The point \(\vek A^k\) is the current design. The grey line is the tangent, that is, the SLP linearization. At \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 300\) mm² the difference is \(2{,}3904 - 2{,}0881 = 0{,}30\) mm: the tangent says \(2{,}088\) mm, but the true displacement is \(2{,}390\) mm. If we draw the same curve against \(1/A_{\mathrm{AC}}\), it is a straight line, and the tangent in this variable lies on the curve.

Definition 29.50 Convex linearization, CONLIN (konveksna linearizacija)

In the setting of definition 29.46 let all areas be strictly positive. An intervening variable is a function \(y_{\mathrm{e}}\) of the area \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) in which we expand the function linearly: \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}\) or \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\). Let \(g\) be one of the functions \(f\), \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\Omega^+ = \{e : \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k) > 0\}\), \(\Omega^- = \{e : \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k) \le 0\}\). The CONLIN approximation of the function \(g\) at \(\vek A^k\) is

\[\tilde g^{\,k}(\vek A) = g(\vek A^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e} \in \Omega^+} \frac{\partial g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e} \in \Omega^-} \frac{\partial g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2\left(\frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{e}}^k} - \frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{e}}}\right) , \tag{29.45}\]

with the derivatives computed at \(\vek A^k\). The variables in which the derivative is positive are expanded in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\), the others in \(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Source: CHK section 4.4 (PDF pp. 67-69): the choice between \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(1/x_{\mathrm{j}}\) by the sign of the derivative, equation (4.5) and the sets \(\Omega_+\), \(\Omega_-\) (PDF p. 69, read by hand from the crop of the equation). The term in \(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the expansion in \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the derivative \(\partial g/\partial y_{\mathrm{e}} = -A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\,\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\) by the chain rule (lemma 8.29).

The name is short for "convex linearization" (CHK PDF p. 68), since the result is a convex function, which we prove at once.

Lemma 29.51 Properties of the CONLIN approximation (lastnosti približka CONLIN)

Let \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) be the CONLIN approximation of definition 29.50 for a continuously differentiable \(g\). Then:

  1. \(\tilde g^{\,k}(\vek A^k) = g(\vek A^k)\) and \(\partial\tilde g^{\,k}/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k) = \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k)\) for every \(e\).
  2. \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) is a convex function on the set of designs with all \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\).
Proof

We must show that the approximation agrees with \(g\) in value and derivative and that it has a nonnegative Hessian matrix, so that by lemma 29.22 it is convex.

  1. At \(\vek A = \vek A^k\) all brackets \((A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)\) and \((1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - 1/A_{\mathrm{e}})\) are zero, so \(\tilde g^{\,k}(\vek A^k) = g(\vek A^k)\).
  2. The derivative with respect to \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) for \(e \in \Omega^+\) is \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\). For \(e \in \Omega^-\) the derivative of the term \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2\,(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - 1/A_{\mathrm{e}})\) with respect to \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k/A_{\mathrm{e}})^2\), because \(\mathrm{d}(-1/A_{\mathrm{e}})/\mathrm{d}A_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\). At \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\) this is again \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\), which completes item 1.
  3. Every term of the sum is a function of one variable, so the Hessian matrix (definition 8.61) is diagonal. For \(e \in \Omega^+\) the second derivative is \(0\), a linear term. For \(e \in \Omega^-\) the second derivative by step 2 is \(-2\,\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2/A_{\mathrm{e}}^3\), and it is \(\ge 0\), because \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} \le 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\).
  4. A diagonal matrix with nonnegative diagonal entries is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), so \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) is convex by lemma 29.22.

Source: CHK section 4.4 (PDF pp. 70-71): the first property and the proof that \(g^{C,k}_{\mathrm{i}}\) is convex, as a sum of terms \(C(x_{\mathrm{j}} - x_{\mathrm{j}}^k)\) and \(A + B/x_{\mathrm{j}}\). The proof with the Hessian matrix, step by step, is ours.

Why the choice by sign? Let us try the opposite, on the volume of bar \(AC\), which is linear in \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) (the derivative \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m is positive). If we expanded it in \(1/A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) we would get \(V_{\mathrm{R}}(A) = L(A^k + (A^k)^2(1/A^k - 1/A))\), that is, \(4\,(1200 - 360\,000/A)\) cm³ for \(A\) in mm² and \(A^k = 600\) mm². The right half of figure 29.25 has axes with the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) horizontal and the volume vertical, negative values included. The blue line is the true volume \(4A\) cm³, the orange curve is \(V_{\mathrm{R}}\), and both pass through the point at \(A^k = 600\) mm² with the same slope \(L = 4\) m. The orange curve is concave: the coefficient \(-L(A^k)^2\) in front of \(1/A\) is negative, so the second derivative is \(-2L(A^k)^2/A^3 < 0\), and at \(A = 1\) mm² the approximation gives the volume \(-1{,}435\cdot 10^{6}\) cm³, a negative one. The subproblem would push the objective toward \(-\infty\) as the area goes to zero, and every bar would vanish. The attempt fails precisely at the point where the lemma demands the sign of the derivative. With the right choice the volume remains a straight line.

Lemma 29.52 CONLIN is exact for a statically determinate truss (CONLIN je točen za statično določeno paličje)

For a statically determinate truss (definition 4.4) with axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\), unit forces \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{e}} = N_{\mathrm{e}} n_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}/E\), the displacement is \(v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\), and its CONLIN approximation at every design with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) is exact if every \(c_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\).

Proof

We must show that the approximation agrees with the function everywhere, not only at \(\vek A^k\).

  1. For a statically determinate truss the equilibrium alone determines \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\), and they do not depend on the areas, so by theorem 4.95 \(v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. Every derivative is \(\partial v/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \le 0\), so all \(e\) lie in \(\Omega^-\).
  3. By formula (29.45), \(\tilde v^{\,k}(\vek A) = v(\vek A^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e}} (-c_{\mathrm{e}}/(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2)(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}) = v(\vek A^k) - \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k + \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Source: The proof is ours. CHK section 4.4 (PDF p. 68) states the same for a statically determinate truss: linearization in \(1/A_{\mathrm{i}}\) is exact, because displacements and stresses are functions of \(1/A_{\mathrm{i}}\).

By lemma 29.52 the displacement of the wall truss is covered by the exact curve, which is the blue curve in the figure. A consequence: the CONLIN subproblem is in this case equal to the true problem. The displacement is exact, and the volume is already linear in the areas (\(L_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\), so all areas are in \(\Omega^+\) for \(f\)). The subproblem is \(\min L_{\mathrm{AC}}A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) subject to \(c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}} \le \delta\).

Example 29.53 One CONLIN step on the wall truss (en korak CONLIN na stenskem paličju)

We solve the subproblem with the multiplier \(\mu\). The problem is convex, since \(V\) is linear and by lemma 29.51 the displacement is convex, so by theorem 29.30 the KKT conditions are sufficient.

  1. Stationarity in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) for the Lagrangian \(V + \mu\,(v - \delta)\): \(L_{\mathrm{e}} - \mu\,c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = 0\), so \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = \sqrt{\mu\,c_{\mathrm{e}}/L_{\mathrm{e}}}\).
  2. The displacement in the constraint: \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \sqrt{c_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}/\mu} = \delta\), so \(\sqrt\mu = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{j}}L_{\mathrm{j}}}/\delta\). The numbers are \(\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{AC}}L_{\mathrm{AC}}} = 1{,}205\cdot 10^{-3}\) m², \(\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{BC}}L_{\mathrm{BC}}} = 1{,}882\cdot 10^{-3}\) m², \(\sqrt\mu = 1{,}5435\) and \(\mu = 2{,}382\) m².
  3. The areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = \sqrt{\mu c_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{AC}}} = 464{,}85\) mm² and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 581{,}07\) mm², the volume \(4764{,}7\) cm³, the displacement \(2{,}0000\) mm. The multiplier is positive.

Since the subproblem at \(\vek A^0 = (600, 600)\) mm² equals the true problem, the result after one round is already the true optimum, and the starting design makes no difference to the areas from CONLIN. SLP did not settle in \(8\) rounds in the same circumstances. The stresses are \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} = -28{,}7\) MPa and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 28{,}7\) MPa: both bars are equally loaded, which is a consequence, not an assumption.

The exactness is a property of static determinacy, not of CONLIN. In a statically indeterminate truss the forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) themselves depend on the areas, so the formula \(v = \sum c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) does not hold and the CONLIN approximation only comes closer. An example is the truss with three bars: the joint \((0, 0)\), supports at \((-1, 1)\), \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\) m, the force \(F = 10\) kN at \(30^\circ\) from the vertical, all areas equal to \(78{,}36\) mm² (volume \(300\) cm³). The compliance \(C\) (section 29.5) there is \(5{,}1625\) J, the derivatives with respect to the areas are \(-E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2L_{\mathrm{e}}\) (corollary 29.44), all negative, so all bars are in \(\Omega^-\). When the area of the first bar is multiplied by \(1{,}5\), the true calculation gives \(C = 3{,}9084\) J, the linear approximation \(3{,}4650\) J (\(-11{,}3\) %) and the CONLIN approximation \(4{,}0308\) J (\(+3{,}1\) %), at half the area (\(\times 0{,}5\)) the true \(7{,}7883\) J, the linear \(6{,}8599\) J (\(-11{,}9\) %) and CONLIN \(8{,}5574\) J (\(+9{,}9\) %). CONLIN is not exact, but in both cases it is closer and above the true value. The linear approximation is below it, as it must be for a convex function: the tangent underestimates it (lemma 29.20). CHK (PDF pp. 69-70) proves that CONLIN is always at least as conservative as SLP.

29.7.4 Moving asymptotes (premikajoče se asimptote)

The method of moving asymptotes (MMA) uses the intervening variables \(1/(A_{\mathrm{e}} - L_{\mathrm{e}})\) and \(1/(U_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}})\), where \(L_{\mathrm{e}} < A_{\mathrm{e}} < U_{\mathrm{e}}\) are asymptotes that move between rounds (CHK section 4.5, PDF pp. 74-76). The first applies to variables with derivative \(\le 0\), the second to those with derivative \(> 0\). The closer the asymptotes lie to the current design, the more conservative the approximation, and the farther away, the more it resembles the tangent plane (PDF pp. 76 and 77). CONLIN is obtained at \(L_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) and \(U_{\mathrm{e}} \to +\infty\), SLP at \(L_{\mathrm{e}} \to -\infty\) and \(U_{\mathrm{e}} \to +\infty\) (PDF p. 77). The asymptotes move by a rule: if the signs of the successive changes \(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k-1}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k-1} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k-2}\) differ, the design variable oscillates and the asymptotes come closer (PDF p. 76), which is exactly the phenomenon of example 29.49. We only state the exact formulas and the proof of convexity, we do not prove them (CHK PDF pp. 74-76). CHK itself mentions that CONLIN sometimes converges slowly or not at all (PDF p. 74), so MMA is an improvement on it.

29.7.5 The optimality criteria update (posodobitev po merilu optimalnosti)

For the problem of the least compliance of a truss at a bounded volume from section 29.5 there is an even simpler loop, which needs no solution of a subproblem. Theorem 29.37 tells us what the optimum looks like: for bars with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) we have \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = \lambda\), for bars without material \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \le \lambda\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the relative elongation of the bar, and \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) is by theorem 4.3 twice the strain energy per volume of the bar, since \(U = EA\varepsilon^2L/2\). The quantity \(\lambda\) here is the multiplier of the volume constraint (in chapter 10 it means an eigenvalue). A bar that stores more energy per volume than the average is too thin, since it has a large elongation, so we thicken it, and conversely. We write this idea as a rule.

Definition 29.54 The optimality criteria update, OC (posodobitev po merilu optimalnosti)

Let the problem be the least compliance of a truss subject to \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}} \le V_0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min} > 0\) (section 29.5). Let \(\vek A^k\) be a design with equilibrium \(\mat K(\vek A^k)\vek u^k = \vek F\) and relative elongations \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^k\), and let \(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2\). Let \(\eta \in (0, 1]\) be a number (the damping) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) a move limit. The optimality criteria update is

\[A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = \min\Big\{\ \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k},\ \max\big\{\ \underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k},\ A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\,(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k/\lambda)^{\eta}\ \big\}\Big\} , \tag{29.46}\]

with the bounds \(\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} = \max\{A_{\min},\ (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\}\) and \(\overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} = (1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\), and with \(\lambda > 0\) chosen so that \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = V_0\).

Source: The form is after CHK section 9.1.2 (PDF p. 191, the equation with \(\eta\), there for a plate with thickness \(x_{\mathrm{e}}\) as the design variable) and SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2, equations (2) and (3), \(\eta = 1/2\), "numerical damping coefficient"). The adaptation to a truss with \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) and volume \(L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is ours: for a bar \(\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^{\T}\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} = E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2L_{\mathrm{e}}\), and dividing by \(a_{\mathrm{e}} = L_{\mathrm{e}}\) leaves \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\).

The name is "criteria" because the rule comes from the criterion of optimality \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = \lambda\) and not from an approximation of the whole problem. We find the value \(\lambda\) by bisection: every term in (29.46) is continuous and does not increase with increasing \(\lambda\), because \(\lambda^{-\eta}\) falls and min and max are not decreasing, so the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1}\) is also continuous and does not increase with \(\lambda\), and the root is found by halving the interval. At \(\eta = 1/2\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}2\) we test the rule on the truss with three bars. Figure 29.26 shows the designs and the quotients through \(30\) rounds.

We start with equal areas \(78{,}36\) mm² (the axes show the area against the round). Then \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = 30{,}6\), \(21{,}4\) and \(0{,}83\) kJ/m³, so the first bar is the most overloaded and the third almost idle. The first bar thickens, the second stays near its start, the third thins toward zero. In the right half the quotients of the first and second bar approach each other and settle at the dashed value \(\lambda \approx 10{,}6\) kJ/m³, and the third falls to zero, that is, below \(\lambda\). After \(30\) rounds the areas are \((155{,}2;\ 80{,}3;\ 0{,}10)\) mm², against the boundary areas of the optimum \((155{,}29;\ 80{,}38;\ 0)\) mm² and the compliance \(3{,}1735\) J (section 29.5). The compliance falls from \(5{,}1625\) J at equal areas to \(3{,}1735\) J, the first six values are \(5{,}1625\), \(4{,}5785\), \(4{,}1905\), \(3{,}9268\), \(3{,}7433\), \(3{,}6115\) J. We are within \(10^{-3}\) of the final value at \(k = 27\), within \(10^{-6}\) at \(k = 56\). Without a move limit (\(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) unbounded) \(5\) rounds sufficed: \(5{,}1625\), \(3{,}6129\), \(3{,}2879\), \(3{,}1870\), \(3{,}1738\), \(3{,}1735\) J. If we put the lower bound at \(1\) mm² instead of nearly zero, the third bar stays at \(1\) mm² and the compliance is \(3{,}1885\) J, which is \(0{,}5\) % larger.

Lemma 29.55 Fixed points of the OC update (negibne točke posodobitve OC)

Let \(A_{\min} > 0\), \(\eta \in (0, 1]\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) and let \(\vek A\) be a design with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min}\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}} = V_0\) and nonsingular \(\mat K(\vek A)\). Then:

  1. If the update (29.46) leaves \(\vek A\) unchanged, \(\vek A^{k+1} = \vek A^k = \vek A\), with some \(\lambda > 0\), then for every \(e\): \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > A_{\min}\) implies \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = \lambda\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\min}\) implies \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \le \lambda\).
  2. If for some \(\lambda > 0\) these two conditions hold, \(\vek A\) is a fixed point of the rule.
  3. Such an \(\vek A\) is a global minimum of the least compliance problem.
Proof

We must show that the fixed points are exactly the points with the criteria of theorem 29.37. We distinguish two cases by bar.

  1. Let \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > A_{\min}\). Then \(\underline A_{\mathrm{e}} < A_{\mathrm{e}} < \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}\), because \(A_{\min} < A_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \((1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}} < A_{\mathrm{e}} < (1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}}\). The result \(\min\{\overline A_{\mathrm{e}}, \max\{\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}, X\}\}\) equals \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) exactly when \(X = A_{\mathrm{e}}\): if \(X < \underline A_{\mathrm{e}}\) or \(X > \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}\), the result is one of the bounds, which differ from \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\), and if \(X\) lies between the bounds, the result is \(X\). So \(A_{\mathrm{e}}(B_{\mathrm{e}}/\lambda)^\eta = A_{\mathrm{e}}\), hence \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = \lambda\) (\(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\)).
  2. Let \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\min}\). The lower bound is \(\max\{A_{\min}, (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\min}\} = A_{\min}\). The result is \(A_{\min}\) exactly when \(A_{\min}(B_{\mathrm{e}}/\lambda)^\eta \le A_{\min}\), that is, \(B_{\mathrm{e}} \le \lambda\).
  3. The conditions are reversible (steps 1 and 2 are equivalences), which is the second claim. The conditions are those of theorem 29.37 with the lower bound \(A_{\min}\), the problem is convex (theorem 29.34), so by theorem 29.30 a fixed point is a global minimum.

Source: The proof is ours. CHK section 9.1.2 (PDF p. 191) states that at convergence the specific strain energy is constant in every element, which is the first condition of the lemma.

A fixed point is therefore an optimum if all bars have \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min} > 0\). The lemma does not say whether the loop reaches a fixed point: convergence is not proved, but in our tests the loop always converged. The lower bound is truly necessary.

Example 29.56 A bar with zero area never returns (palica z ničelno ploščino se ne vrne)

Take the same truss with three bars and the force at \(30^\circ\) and a starting design in which the middle bar is removed: \((106{,}07;\ 0;\ 106{,}07)\) mm², volume \(300\) cm³. The matrix \(\mat K\) is nonsingular, since bars \(1\) and \(3\) lie at \(\pm 45^\circ\). If the lower bound is \(A_{\min} = 0\), the right-hand side of (29.46) at \(A_2 = 0\) is \(0\cdot(B_2/\lambda)^\eta = 0\) for every \(B_2\), so the middle bar stays zero forever. The loop converges to the design \((167{,}30;\ 0;\ 44{,}83)\) mm² with compliance \(5{,}1020\) J, not to \(3{,}1735\) J. The condition of the lemma is violated there: \(E\varepsilon_2^2 = 68{,}03\) kJ/m³ is larger than \(\lambda = 17{,}007\) kJ/m³, the middle bar should receive material but cannot. With \(A_{\min} = 10^{-4}\) mm² (and a move limit) the same start converges to \((155{,}29;\ 80{,}38;\ 0)\) mm² and \(3{,}1735\) J, because the result of expression (29.46) at \(A_2 = A_{\min}\) can grow up to \((1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\min}\) and onward.

Programs therefore always use a positive lower bound, even for bars that should vanish. A consequence is that at \(A_{\min} = 1\) mm² the compliance is \(0{,}5\) % above the optimum, so we choose the lower bound small.

CHK (PDF pp. 186-191) shows that OC is a special case of sequential convex approximations: it linearizes the compliance in the intervening variable \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}^{-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha > 0\), at \(\alpha = 1\) this is CONLIN (PDF p. 186), and the damping is \(\eta = 1/(1 + \alpha)\) (PDF p. 191). Our \(\eta = 1/2\) is therefore CONLIN. We state this, we do not prove it.

Open questions. We tested the loops SLP and OC on small trusses with two and three bars, their convergence is not proved, and it is not proved for larger problems. How OC performs when the variable is the area of an element on a plate and the bars number in the thousands is shown by section 29.9, where the same rule solves a problem of topology.

29.8 The stiffest rod (najtogejša palica)

So far a design variable (projektna spremenljivka) was a list of numbers, for example the areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) of two bars of a truss. Let us ask what happens when a single rod has its own area in every cross-section. Then the area is not a number but a function \(A(x)\) of the distance \(x\) from the support, and each of its infinitely many values may be chosen separately. When the design variable is a function, we speak of a distributed parameter system (sistem s porazdeljenimi parametri), because the decision is spread along the whole length and not collected in a few numbers. A truss is by nature a discrete system, because there are as many variables as there are bars (CHK §1.5, PDF p. 17). The stiffest (najtogejša) rod is the one with the greatest stiffness among all those with the same volume of material. We measure stiffness by compliance (podajnost, section 29.5): the more stiffness, the less compliance.

The model is this. A straight rod of length \(L\) is clamped into a wall at \(x = 0\), is free at \(x = L\), and on every unit of length of the rod acts a force \(b(x)\) in the direction of the \(x\) axis. We call such a force a distributed load (porazdeljena obtežba), because it is not concentrated at one point but spread over the whole rod. Its unit is N/m. In chapter 11 the letter \(b\) means force per unit volume, here it is force per unit length. There are three idealizations. The material is linearly elastic with modulus \(E\) (definition 3.1), displacements are small, and the load \(b\) does not depend on the area, as the weight of the rod would. The weight of a rod of volume \(100\) cm³ is \(7{,}65\) N, which is \(0{,}08\) % of the load \(10\) kN we shall take below, so we neglect it. For \(b\) we assume that it is continuous and that there is a number \(m > 0\) with \(b(x) \ge m\) everywhere, so the rod is pulled everywhere (tension, section 2.1).

Let us draw the rod as on a board. The wall is on the left, because the rod is clamped there. The rod reaches from it to the free end. We draw the load as a row of arrows on the axis of the rod, because the axis is the line along which the forces act, and each arrow pulls in the direction of \(x\). The forces act along the axis, so in a cross-section only the axial force matters (definition 2.5). How large is it in the cross-section at \(x\)? We cut the rod in thought at \(x\), at the distance \(x\) from the wall, and look at the piece from the cut to the free end, which we draw separately. Only two forces act on it. The first is the load on the piece, whose sum is \(b\,(L - x)\) if \(b\) is constant. The second is the axial force across the cut. By definition 2.5 the part on the side of larger \(x\) acts on the part on the side of smaller \(x\) with the force \(N\), so the part on the side of smaller \(x\) acts on our piece with the force \(-N(x)\) in the direction of \(x\), that is, it pulls the piece to the left, and the arrow is drawn from the cut to the left. The piece is in equilibrium (definition 2.3), the sum of the forces on it is zero, and the load on the piece is the integral of the load over it. Therefore

\[N(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L b(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{29.47}\]

For a constant load \(b\) we have \(N(x) = b\,(L - x)\), from \(bL\) at the wall to \(0\) at the free end. Always \(N(x) \ge m\,(L - x) \ge 0\) (lemma 3.39, item 3). It matters that we obtained \(N\) from equilibrium alone, without the area and the material. We call such a rod statically determinate (statično določena): the forces in it are determined by statics, that is, by equilibrium, hence the name. What would be different is shown by the example of a rod clamped at both ends, at the end of the section.

Now we know where the force is large. At the wall the cross-section carries the whole load, at the free end almost nothing. Let us test what that means on a steel rod with \(E = 196\) GPa (section 3.1.5), length \(L = 1\) m, load \(b = 10\) kN/m and constant area \(A_0 = 100\) mm². The volume is \(V = A_0 L = 100\) cm³. The stress (definition 2.6) is \(bL/A_0 = 100\) MPa at the wall, zero at the free end, and in between it falls linearly. The material near the free end hardly carries anything, and the material at the wall carries the most. How could we redistribute the same material so that the rod is as stiff as possible?

In section 29.5 the compliance is the number \(F\cdot u\), the force times its displacement. We cut the load into pieces: the piece at \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) of length \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) has the force \(b(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and its displacement is \(u(x_{\mathrm{i}})\). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} b(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,u(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a Riemann sum (definition 3.32) and approaches an integral.

Definition 29.57 Compliance of a rod under a distributed load (podajnost palice pod porazdeljeno obtežbo)

Let a rod be clamped at \(x = 0\), with the load \(b\) and the displacement \(u(x)\) of the cross-section at \(x\), continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\). The compliance (podajnost) of the rod is the number

\[C = \int_0^L b(x)\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{29.48}\]

Source: CHK §8.3 (PDF pp. 168 and 173): compliance is the value \(\ell(U)\) of the linear form of the load at the equilibrium displacement and by (8.26) equals \(a(U, U)\). For a rod \(\ell(v) = \int b\,v\,\mathrm{d}x\) (PDF p. 173). For point forces it is the \(F\cdot u\) of section 29.5.

Compliance depends on the area, because the displacement \(u\) depends on it, so we write \(C(A)\) when we stress this. Which areas may we choose? Those that nowhere break the rod where there is force, and that near the free end, where there is hardly any force, may be arbitrarily small.

Definition 29.58 Admissible area function (dopustna funkcija ploščine)

Let a rod be as above, with the axial force \(N\) from equation (29.47). A function \(A : [0, L] \to [0, \infty)\) is an admissible area function (dopustna funkcija ploščine) if it satisfies three conditions:

  1. \(A\) is continuous on \([0, L]\),
  2. \(A(x) > 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L)\),
  3. the stress \(\sigma(x) = N(x)/A(x)\) on \([0, L)\) has a limit as \(x\) tends to \(L\) (definition 1.5).

We take the value of this limit as \(\sigma(L)\).

Source: The notion is not from the source. CHK §8.3 (PDF p. 169) requires only \(\rho \ge 0\) and a given volume.

The name admissible says that the function may take part in the contest for the best, like the elements of the feasible set in section 29.1. Condition 2 does not allow the rod to be broken anywhere, because the elongation there would be infinite. Condition 3 does not allow infinite stress at the free end. Two properties follow from it that we shall need. First, \(\sigma\) is continuous on \([0, L]\): on \([0, L)\) as a quotient of continuous functions with a denominator that is not zero (lemma 4.108, item 2), and at \(L\) by the choice of \(\sigma(L)\) (definition 1.58). Second, \(N = \sigma A\) on \([0, L]\): on \([0, L)\) by the definition of \(\sigma\), and at \(L\) the left side is zero, and so is the right, because either \(A(L) = 0\), or \(A(L) > 0\) and \(\sigma(L) = \lim N/A = 0/A(L) = 0\).

How do we compute the compliance without computing the displacement? The load is known, the axial force is given by equation (29.47), and the displacement follows from the strain. With integration by parts we move the derivative from \(u\) to \(N\).

Lemma 29.59 Compliance of a statically determinate rod (podajnost statično določene palice)

Let a rod be as above with an admissible area function \(A\) and displacement \(u\), \(u(0) = 0\). Then
